| Weight | 13.64 pounds (6.2kg) | 
| Warranty | 3 years | 
The M10S II starts with an OLED panel that runs natively at 2560x1440 QHD resolution and 540 Hz. A dual-refresh mode bumps that up to 720 Hz at HD, 1280x720 pixels. Adaptive-Sync runs on both AMD and Nvidia platforms, and you get HDR support with the ability to calibrate for HDR10 content. The screen coating is unusual in that it’s matte, while nearly every OLED that crosses my desk is shiny. That finish is extremely effective at rejecting image-spoiling ambient light. It literally swallows up reflections and displays the image without any visible grain.
The M10S II delivers a huge color gamut that, in my tests, covered nearly 110% of DCI-P3. I found that calibration was necessary, but the reward was a beautifully saturated image. There’s an sRGB mode available if you need that smaller gamut for photography or graphics work. You also get variable brightness to stretch dynamic range. It has two settings that had a positive impact in both practice and testing. I’ll tell you more about that on page four. Peak output is around 475 nits in SDR mode and 543 nits in HDR mode when measuring a 25% window pattern.
For gaming, you get plenty of goodness in the form of static and dynamic aiming points, OLED anti-flicker, black frame insertion for blur reduction at low frame rates, an FPS indicator, and a set of timers. Missing are internal speakers and LED lighting, but you do get USB ports for peripherals. There’s panel protection in the form of advanced heat management and OLED care options, such as panel refresh and pixel orbiting. The latest I/O ports also include one DisplayPort 2.1 and two HDMI 2.1 ports. A pair of headphones can be plugged into the provided 3.5mm jack. There’s a comprehensive OSD for control, or you can use Sony’s INZONE Hub app, which is free to download.
The M10S II sells for $1,100 at this writing, so it’s primed to compete with other speedy competition displays. While it isn’t quite as loaded as an Asus ROG Swift screen, it delivers equal performance and image quality.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Assembly and Accessories
The M10S II’s carton gets the full cardboard treatment with no crumbly foam in sight. The panel, upright, and base assemble without tools. If you plan to use an arm, there’s a 100mm VESA mount with fasteners included. Also in the box are a DisplayPort cable, an external power brick, and a sheet of INZONE stickers, in case you want to decorate your Trapper Keeper.
Product 360
The M10S II’s most visible feature is its small-footprint base. Honestly, when I took it out of the box, I was dubious about its stability. It’s a heavy metal disc just six inches across. The upright bolts to its center with an offset that extends the depth to almost eight inches. It looks like it would fall over easily, but I gave it a few shakes, and it remained stable. This is geometry at work. The swivel point is where the upright and base meet, allowing you to swing the screen 360 degrees. You also get a 5/35-degree tilt and a 4.8-inch height range, no portrait mode, though. Movements are firm and smooth with no wobble or play.
Reach around the back right, and you’ll find a small protrusion with a power button and a joystick for the OSD. Uniquely, the power LED is positioned on the side, just the right spot to light up your hand when you press the button. It isn’t visible from the front, but you can turn it off if you wish.
The side view shows a thick component bulge attached to a thin screen backed by a metal plate. It’s just 5mm thick, and the bezel is narrow too: 7mm on top, 8mm on the sides, and 12mm at the bottom. It’s flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off.
The I/O panel is up and under and includes two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and USB, one upstream and two downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, so you can plug headphones into the 3.5mm jack. An additional USB port is there for service and firmware updates.
OSD Features
Pressing the M10S II’s joystick brings up an efficiently organized OSD. It’s divided into nine sections and has plenty of calibration and convenience options.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The OSD begins with picture modes, eight in total. The default is Game, and it looks good but needs a bit of tweaking to align it with broadcast standards. The other modes are aimed at specific game types or tasks, and there’s an accurate sRGB mode. I found the best results using Standard with a grayscale calibration, which you can read about below and on page four.
Gaming Assist includes the refresh rate switches and 24.5-inch modes which deliver 1080 vertical pixels while maintaining a 1:1 mapping. That way, there’s no scaling to soften the image. You also get motion blur reduction via a backlight strobe, which works well at low frame rates. It cuts brightness by around 30%. Anti-VRR flicker is unique to OLED monitors and prevents flickering during rapid frame-rate transitions. Hint: if your video card is fast enough to keep the action above 300 Hz, you won’t get flicker. Also in this menu are an FPS counter and aiming points, both static and dynamic.
In the Picture adjustment menu, you’ll find the variable brightness options, which Sony calls Brightness stabilizer. It’s counter to other monitors I’ve encountered, in that off means variable brightness is fully engaged. I experimented with all three settings and found the best gamma, and therefore quality, on the Mid setting. Also, here are gamma presets and color temps with a set of RGB sliders. There is no color gamut selector, but you can opt for sRGB in the sRGB picture mode.
For panel care, the M10S II includes pixel shift, a screen saver, and refresh routines. Sony differentiates between pixel and panel refresh. I ran the pixel refresh when I first powered up my sample. Selecting panel refresh prompted a message that it should only be run once a year, so I concluded it was a very aggressive refresh routine.
Sony INZONE M10S II Calibration Settings
The M10S II arrived set to its Game mode, which had a cool grayscale and light gamma. I could fix the grayscale but not the gamma, so I turned to Standard mode, which was much better. After a few clicks of the RGB sliders, I had much improved grayscale, gamma, and color tracking. The gamut volume is just under 110% of DCI-P3, which is too large for the SDR standard but looks great, nonetheless. If you want sRGB, it’s there in the preset mode list. It has good gamut accuracy and supports grayscale calibration but not gamma adjustment. My recommended settings are below.
For HDR content, the M10S II switches over automatically and provides four specific picture modes. Game works the best, and I noted that it allowed grayscale calibration and brightness adjustment. You can see those test results on page five.
| Picture Mode | Standard | 
| Brightness 200 nits | 51 | 
| Brightness 120 nits | 28 | 
| Brightness 100 nits | 23 | 
| Brightness 80 nits | 17 | 
| Brightness 50 nits | 8 (min. 22 nits) | 
| Contrast | 75 | 
| Gamma | 2.2 | 
| Color Temp User | Red 100, Green 100, Blue 98 | 
Gaming and Hands-on
Sony’s marketing for the M10S II clearly targets competition and hardcore gamers, and for those users, it delivers. Whether you need 540 Hz or not, it is super quick. Motion resolution is perfect, which means moving objects and backgrounds have the same clarity as stationary elements. Camera pans are free from blur or smearing. Adaptive-Sync worked perfectly for me when using a GeForce RTX 4090 video card. Frame rates in Doom Eternal set to max detail ranged from 350 to 540fps.
The M10S II has a couple of features designed to reduce motion blur and smooth out the image, but I didn’t find any need for them. Anti-flicker, which I’ve seen from Asus as well, is there to remove any flickering during frame rate transitions. I saw plenty of those with rates rapidly shifting 80-100fps by the second. There was no flicker. You also get blur reduction via backlight strobe. It only works below 270 Hz, and since my speeds never went below that, it wasn’t needed. To engage it, turn off Adaptive-Sync first. The M10S II will automatically reduce the refresh rate. It works well and shows no evidence of phasing or ghosting.
Input lag is low enough that I perceived instant response to control inputs during the most frenetic battle maneuvers. My skills are average, but I see this monitor’s benefit to a competitive gamer. The 720 Hz mode felt super quick even though its input lag is only a tad lower. Full-screen resolution is limited to 1280x720, but you can achieve dizzying frame rates in the process. Also available are 24.5-inch modes in which the picture occupies a portion of the screen. You can do 1920x1080 at 720 Hz this way or opt for 2368x1332 pixels in a 1:1 mapping.
In all scenarios, color and clarity are as good as it gets for the OLED genre. The M10S II has a huge color gamut, almost 110% of DCI-P3, and that shows in both SDR and HDR content. HDR has the additional capability of calibration, something most HDR monitors cannot do. I also liked the variable brightness options. The terminology is a little counterintuitive in that when Brightness stabilizer is off, variable brightness is engaged at maximum. The other settings, Mid and High, are less aggressive at modulating light output. I found the best gamma, and therefore picture quality, came from the Mid option.
As a 27-inch QHD flat panel, the M10S II is well suited for productivity and delivers a clean and colorful picture for general use. Small text is sharp and free of color fringing. Graphics and photos are deeply textured, and video looks great as well. The monitor makes a great personal TV. The only things I noted missing were internal speakers and LED lighting. But everything you need for gaming, entertainment, and work is there.
Takeaway: The M10S II is a competitor’s dream with its speedy response, smooth motion resolution, and multitude of refresh and resolution options. It delivers a clean and colorful picture for both SDR and HDR content. The anti-glare layer is among the best I’ve seen, with no effects seen from ambient light reflections. It’s a premium purchase for sure, but there is nothing it cannot do well.

articles.title: KDE Begins Drafting AI Guidelines: "Don't Be a Meat Proxy"
articles.text:
Wednesday, September 23rd 2026
	
									
	
	
	
KDE Begins Drafting AI Guidelines: "Don't Be a Meat Proxy"
Despite the immense popularity of LLMs and AI coding agents in software development, the open-source community seems to be quite divided on the topic at times. On the one hand, you have projects like GIMP banning AI from its codebase entirely, while other projects, like Nobara Linux and Omarchy, are very much all-in on AI coding. There is, however, a middle ground, like the Linux Kernel project, which allows AI-assisted and -generated code in the codebase, but all code requires human review and a proper merge request write-up that demonstrates an understanding of the actual code submitted. This appears to be where KDE Plasma will land as a project, if the recent proposed KDE LLM guidelines are anything to go by. 
The draft of KDE's LLM guidelines was submitted for discussion by project lead, Nate Graham, and it outlines rules that effectively summarized by the golden rule: "Don't be lazy." In the KDE LLM guidelines discussion post, the proposed draft explains that "contributions with obvious and lazy LLM usage may be ignored or closed," and that "nobody should know if you use an LLM," because the output should be indistinguishable from what you could produce yourself without an LLM. It also places rules on AI-generated text, forbidding AI-generated text for merge requests, commit messages, or replying to a question or comment. The current draft also seeks to prevent additional work being placed on maintainers by limiting vibe-coded changes to that maintainers are expected to clean up and implement—an issue faced by Godot maintainers not long ago.KDE will seemingly also expect developers to take responsibility for their LLM-generated code, with the draft guidelines specifically forbidding adding AI disclosures as a way to excuse low-quality work. The draft has yet to be finalized, and the discussion around the LLM guidelines is expected to continue in the upcoming days, after which a finalized version will be added to the KDE documentation. The full KDE LLM Guidelines follows:
LLM usage
		
		Source:
				KDE Invent			
	
	
	
		
	
		
The draft of KDE's LLM guidelines was submitted for discussion by project lead, Nate Graham, and it outlines rules that effectively summarized by the golden rule: "Don't be lazy." In the KDE LLM guidelines discussion post, the proposed draft explains that "contributions with obvious and lazy LLM usage may be ignored or closed," and that "nobody should know if you use an LLM," because the output should be indistinguishable from what you could produce yourself without an LLM. It also places rules on AI-generated text, forbidding AI-generated text for merge requests, commit messages, or replying to a question or comment. The current draft also seeks to prevent additional work being placed on maintainers by limiting vibe-coded changes to that maintainers are expected to clean up and implement—an issue faced by Godot maintainers not long ago.KDE will seemingly also expect developers to take responsibility for their LLM-generated code, with the draft guidelines specifically forbidding adding AI disclosures as a way to excuse low-quality work. The draft has yet to be finalized, and the discussion around the LLM guidelines is expected to continue in the upcoming days, after which a finalized version will be added to the KDE documentation. The full KDE LLM Guidelines follows:
LLM usage
The golden rule for LLM usage in KDE is Don't be lazy:
The result will be poor-quality work that eventually becomes someone else's problem.
- Don't try to use a tool to replace your own judgment, interpersonal communication, or learning process.
- Don't take unsustainable shortcuts.
- Don't avoid growing as a person.
Nobody in KDE should know if you use an LLM—not because you're concealing it, but because your usage of it produces output indistinguishable from what you could produce yourself. Contributions with obvious and lazy LLM usage may be ignored or closed.
Using an LLM to generate contributions
KDE follows a "human in the loop" principle: you must be making decisions and adjustments beyond mere prompting. The output must express your unique humanity in some way.
Don't be a "meat proxy". For example:
Using an LLM to generate text
- Don't submit "vibe-coded" changes you don't understand and couldn't make yourself.
- Don't submit throwaway LLM-created changes as a "first draft or proof-of-concept for maintainers to improve".
- Don't disclose LLM usage as a way of trying to excuse the potential errors or poor quality of a contribution that you haven't put much effort into.
- Don't add "Assisted-by: [some LLM]" tags to your commits; it's just free advertising for the LLM's provider.
Generally, don't.
What you are willing to write is generally the upper limit of what others are willing to read.
LLMs, on the other hand, often produce long, rambling, soulless, corporate-sounding nonsense that nobody wants to read; don't do it. This includes:
The one acceptable usage is to write text in your native language and then machine-translate it into English, with no stylistic or tonal changes.
- Don't use an LLM to "organize your thoughts" and copy-paste the output somewhere. Organize them yourself.
- Don't use an LLM to generate commit messages and merge request descriptions. Write them yourself.
- Don't use an LLM to generate a reply to someone's question or comment, then copy-paste that as if it were your response. Understand and reply yourself.
Other usage of LLMs
If you use an LLM to debug issues or find bugs, make sure its conclusion is correct.
If you use an LLM for research, or to replace reading API docs directly, verify the accuracy of what it told you.

articles.title: The old cybersecurity model is breaking | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even seeing companies like Instinct and Simile bring in nine-figure checks and valuations that wouldn’t have made sense a few years ago.
With a front row seat to it all is Shardul Shah, a partner at Index Ventures who’s spent nearly two decades investing in cybersecurity and enterprise software — including six consecutive rounds in cloud security startup Wiz, which Google acquired for $32 billion earlier this year in one of its largest acquisitions ever.
On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Shah joins Rebecca Bellan to break down why he thinks periodic, human-in-the-loop security can’t keep up anymore, and why Index continues investing in AI-native security companies at stages that once required much more proof.

articles.title: The Download: a bid to scrap the virtual wall and AI hits Climate Week
articles.text:
The Download: a bid to scrap the virtual wall and AI hits Climate Week
Plus: an OpenAI agent has executed the first known AI hack of a government site.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program
Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced plans to introduce legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along the country’s southern border.
The announcement comes just days after publication of an MIT Technology Review investigation, “Dying on Camera,” which looked at deaths near these towers. Nearly one in four deaths we analyzed between 2015 and early 2026 occurred within their advertised range.
Ramirez, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee, cited our reporting that nearly “1,100 people have died within range of a billion-dollar surveillance tower system between 2015 and 2026,” adding, “The towers that we have paid a billion dollars to just don’t work.”
Here’s what she’s proposing and what it could mean for the border surveillance program.
—Eileen Guo
Read all of MIT Technology Review’s groundbreaking “virtual wall” investigation here.
Roundtables: the deadly failures of the virtual border wall
The US spent billions building the “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border, promising they will help detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives. But MIT Technology Review has documented more than a thousand people who moved through areas watched by these towers without being caught—and ultimately died there.
Next Monday, join our editor-in-chief Mat Honan, senior AI reporter James O’Donnell, and senior reporter for features and investigations Eileen Guo for a subscriber-only conversation about the investigation. They’ll examine the failures of border surveillance technology and uncover the stories of the people who die in the borderlands.
Register now to attend on Monday, September 28 at 19:00 BST / 2:00pm EDT / 11:00am PDT.
Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.
AI is dominating the conversation at Climate Week
—Casey Crownhart
AI is the unavoidable topic at this year’s New York Climate Week, with tension growing over its costs and benefits.
The technology is attracting more attention and money to energy technologies, some of which are low- or zero-emission. But the data center buildout has come with a hefty environmental toll, and a whole lot of natural gas is coming online to meet the demand.
Overall, what I’m hearing this week is that many in the climate sector are skeptical of AI, at best. Find out why.
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 An OpenAI agent has executed the first known AI hack of a government site
It breached an Australian government health data portal in June. (CNN)
+ OpenAI notified Australia three months later through a public mailbox. (BBC)
+ No patient records are believed to have been accessed. (Guardian)
+ Its agents also tried to breach three other sites. (NYT $)
+ Here's why AI agents cheat to reach their goals. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Data stolen in the FBI hack exposes agents’ sensitive intelligence roles
It identifies staff working on China, Russia, and cyber. (Reuters $)
+ And may have exposed the FBI’s own hacking unit. (404 Media)
+ The group behind the incident claims it isn’t financially motivated. (Register)
3 The US rejected calls from OpenAI and Anthropic for global AI standards
A Trump advisor said global rules threatened the country’s AI lead. (BBC)
+ America’s AI leaders had urged the UN to coordinate on safety. (Gizmodo)
+ The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. (MIT Technology Review)
4 Meta has unveiled new AI glasses—and a pendant for Muse
Camera-free smart glasses address growing privacy concerns. (Verge)
+ While the Muse Charm enables hands-free interaction with the AI agent. (BBC)
+ Mark Zuckerberg wants Muse to be a "personal superintelligence.” (Axios)
+ Meta also showed off new VR glasses. (CNBC)
5 China is accelerating its AI push ahead of the Xi-Trump summit
Huawei and Alibaba have both unveiled new flagship chips. (CNBC)
+ The country’s AI industry has shrugged off America’s safety panic. (Atlantic $)
+ The US leads in AI models, but China has talent and political edges. (NYT $)
+ Chinese models have divided the White House. (MIT Technology Review)
6 US lawmakers have proposed new rules for blocking Chinese tech
The bipartisan bill would require broader review of national security risks. (Hill)
+ And give Congress the power to overturn FCC bans. (Reuters $)
7 Tech giants have urged Trump to withdraw $103,265 H-1B fee
They say the charge could weaken US competitiveness. (WSJ $)
8 Scientists have detected radio signals from an exoplanet for the first time
The signals likely come from intense magnetic activity on the planet. (Wired $)
9 An invisible force has a mysterious effect on aging
Shielding fruit flies from Earth’s magnetic field changed their lifespans. (404 Media)
10 ‘Dopamine sites’ are recreating the thrill of shopping without paying
FoodNeverComes has attracted more than 2.7 million visitors since June. (BBC)
Quote of the day
"They decided to break the law."
—Ed Santow, co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, tells ABC radio why there should be serious legal consequences for OpenAI agents hacking Australia's Medicare statistics portal.
One more thing
The quest to figure out farming on Mars
If ever a blade of grass grew on Mars, those days are over. But could they begin again? What would it take to grow plants to feed future astronauts on Mars?
To grow food there, we can’t just drop seeds in the ground and add water. We will need to create a layer of soil that can support life. And to do that, we first have to get rid of the red planet’s toxic salts.
Researchers recently discovered a potential solution—and the early signs are promising. Read the full story.
—David W. Brown
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ Meet Alfie, a dog with flowing locks that croons like an opera singer.
+ Watch the 100 wildest homemade plane flights and crashes from Red Bull Flugtag.
+ Marmot researchers have launched OnlyMarms, a free, G-rated account of cute videos that funds their work through tips.
+ The full trailer for Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary is here, and somehow it looks even weirder than expected.

articles.title: Here's the Torcal, the first fully electric Bentley
articles.text:
A few weeks ago, Bentley gave Ars a ride in a new camouflaged electric vehicle. Named after a Spanish rock formation, the Torcal is the brand’s first battery EV, and today the production car had its formal unveiling. That camo was effective: The real car is less bulbous and more blocky than its disguise would suggest. And it’s fair to say it brings some of the ideas of the EXP 15 concept to the road—even if that didn’t include that show car’s elegant, stretched proportions. It’s smaller than the Bentayga, and it should slot beneath that model in pricing (or the PHEV version of it, at least), though Bentley has yet to reveal exactly how much US buyers can expect to pay.
Underneath the bodywork are some relatively familiar underpinnings; Bentley shares technology with Porsche as both are part of the greater Volkswagen Group empire. The power output might not be as prodigious as the electric Porsche Cayenne but should be sufficient nonetheless. The standard car will offer peak outputs of 810 hp (604 kW) and 880 lb-ft (1,194 Nm), enough for a 3.3-second 0–60 mph time (0–100 km/h takes 3.4 seconds).
The more powerful Torcal S boasts 875 hp (653 kW) and 995 lb-ft (1,350 Nm) at its most potent; this is capable of 60 mph from a standing start in a mere 2.8 seconds (2.9 to 100 km/h) and an increased top speed of 162 mph (260 km/h), up from 155 mph (250 km/h) for the standard version, either of which are academic outside certain stretches of German highway.
Although it’s a much heavier car, the Torcal’s suspension and drive modes have been tuned to be familiar to existing customers, including things like pedal calibrations and steering response rates. And the clever active ride suspension means the Torcal isn’t just a one-trick wonder. “[In] a steady state environment… you’ve got the ride comfort and compliance from a Flying Spur, but in a dynamic environment, we’ve got a vehicle that’s as dynamic and capable as a GT,” said Martin Page, product line director for the Torcal.

articles.title: Control Resonant gets tough, but gives you the tools to deal with it
articles.text:
Control Resonant isn’t an easy game. At any given moment while exploring vast open areas where you’re sometimes leaping from wall to wall to ceiling, you may be surrounded by swarms of otherworldly enemies trying to crush you into the ground. It can be a lot, especially when enemies sometimes take a long time to take down. I died often. But whenever I got to a point where I was starting to feel frustrated, I didn’t have to suffer for too long; thanks to Resonant’s generous assist mode, I often tweaked the game’s settings to give me an edge so that I could keep on trucking through the game’s weird world.
Control Resonant gets tough, but gives you the tools to deal with it
Remedy’s Control sequel has a generous assist mode that lets you tweak the difficulty whenever you want.
The assist mode is accessible from Control Resonant’s pause menu. You can tweak things like how much damage you give and take or how generous of a window you have for pulling off dodges, and you can even give yourself immortality or the ability to pull off one-hit kills. There are also a few presets that are a bit like traditional difficulty options if you don’t want to get too deep into messing with the sliders. While the game encourages you to try playing with assist mode disabled, there’s no penalty to flipping it on, and you don’t even need to reload your game if you do so.
I started using assist mode quite early. Initially, you don’t have many combat abilities or passive skills to make fighting easier, and I was regularly getting my clock cleaned. But with a few small adjustments in assist mode, I made myself just a little bit more powerful while not completely removing any challenge, which kept fights engaging at a pace that felt right to me. After a few hours of leveling up, I noticed I was starting to coast, so I turned assist mode off to bring the difficulty back up.
I found myself toggling assist mode in different ways as I played. Resonant throws a lot of bad guys at you, and I sometimes found the combat to be pretty boring. But instead of resigning myself to slogging through frustrating fights that blocked me from seeing the trippy story beats and locations that I love about Remedy games, I’d adjust some assist mode settings, take out the enemies in my way, and move on to the good stuff. This was a particularly good approach for Resonant’s bosses, which are awe-inspiring spectacles but feature giant health bars; I’d usually start a fight with assist mode disabled and incrementally tweak settings in my favor every time I died so that I could still feel the thrill of a fight without completely eliminating the challenge.
Assist mode was also great for more efficiently tackling Resonant’s sprawling maps, which are littered with secrets and quests. In one area, I had to track down a bunch of chunks of weird mold that protagonist Dylan felt compelled to eat. (It’s gross, but it makes sense in context, I promise.) When I first understood the scope of the mission, I wasn’t looking forward to it; I figured the quest waypoints would all be guarded by hordes of enemies that I didn’t really want to deal with. I just wanted to learn about the mold. But by flipping on immortality and one-hit kills, I blasted through the boring fights so that I could more quickly get to the mold and the narrative reveals that followed. When I got to the (satisfyingly stomach-turning) boss at the end of the quest, I turned off my superpowers so I could take it on.
Control Resonant has a little too much bloat; there are too many enemies wandering the maps and too many open-world activities to sort through. The game’s combat isn’t interesting enough, like in a FromSoftware title or Capcom’s recent Onimusha: Way of the Sword, to make suffering feel worth it. It also, like the original Control, suffers from big difficulty spikes. Remedy patched an assist mode into Control after launch, and with Resonant, it’s including one right from the start. The feature let me set my own pace so that I could see the best parts of the game, which is filled with mind-bending set-pieces and twists, on my own terms.

articles.title: ChatGPT Voice da un salto y ahora puede manejar tu correo y tu agenda mientras hablas
articles.text:
ChatGPT está a nada de convertirse en Samantha, la asistente de voz que interpretó Scarlett Johansson en Her. OpenAI lanzó una actualización en todas las plataformas que unifica las funciones de texto, voz y trabajo agéntico en una sola experiencia. La nueva versión ya está disponible en móviles, la web y la aplicación de escritorio para que conversemos con la IA de forma más natural.
De acuerdo con una publicación en la cuenta de X de OpenAI, ChatGPT Voice ya funciona con GPT-6 Astra, Sol y Luna. Si bien Astra ya llevaba algunas semanas disponible, Sol y Luna recibieron su actualización apenas ayer. Con esta integración, los usuarios ya podrán acceder a un nivel de inteligencia mayor al hablar con el asistente de voz y realizar alguna pregunta.
Otro cambio importante tiene que ver con los plugins. Una de las mayores limitantes del modo de voz de ChatGPT es que no podía acceder a integraciones como el correo, calendario o Slack al conversar con el usuario. OpenAI eliminó esa barrera y ahora los usuarios podrán gestionar la agenda, redactar un correo o resumir un chat de Slack a través del modo de voz, sin necesidad de que ChatGPT tenga que cambiar a texto.
La actualización también añade ChatGPT Work, el sistema agéntico de OpenAI pensado para realizar tareas más complejas, en la misma interfaz de usuario. Ahora puedes crear documentos, armar presentaciones o construir una hoja de cálculo simplemente hablando con la IA, ya sea desde la web o en la aplicación móvil. Esta integración acerca a ChatGPT Work a lo que Codex ofrece en escritorio, aunque con la ventaja de que está disponible en más plataformas.
OpenAI apuesta con todo por el modo de voz en ChatGPT
No es un secreto que Sam Altman y compañía quieran replicar lo que se vio en Her, la película de Spike Jonze que se estrenó hace más de una década. En ese tiempo, la idea de una asistente con IA que nos acompañara a todos lados y que fuera capaz de formar un vínculo con nosotros se encontraba en el terreno de la ciencia ficción. Pero años más tarde llegó ChatGPT y las cosas cambiaron, sobre todo cuando debutó el modo de voz que clonó de forma arbitraria la voz de Scarlett Johansson.
Hace unos meses, OpenAI presentó GPT-Live-1, un modelo de voz con capacidades para hablar y escuchar al mismo tiempo. Este modelo sustituyó el viejo esquema de tres piezas independientes (voz a texto, generación de respuesta y texto a voz) por un sistema más fluido, capaz de guardar silencio y de absorber contexto hasta que se le necesita. Atty Eleti, líder de producto de ChatGPT Voice, dijo durante la presentación de julio que GPT-Live-1 le permitió lograr conversaciones de hasta 40 minutos con la IA.
Con el lanzamiento de hoy, OpenAI se acerca cada vez más a ese futuro que solo veíamos en películas. La compañía dijo que, con el tiempo, la voz será la interfaz principal para tareas complejas y de larga duración para ChatGPT.

articles.title: Femtech Connect conference puts femtech funding under the microscope | BetaKit
articles.text:
Women founders dominate the landscape in the growing femtech sector, but their male counterparts still receive the lion’s share of investment dollars. Changing that disparity was a major focus on Monday during Femtech Connect, a national femtech summit launched by the newly minted venture firm Antigoni Studios.
“We know there’s a significant white space where women are driving really compelling innovation, and it has been undercapitalized.”
Antigoni is an Edmonton-based firm with national ambitions that claims to be Canada’s first femtech-exclusive VC firm. Femtech is the broad term for technology that addresses the health and wellness needs that disproportionately impact women, girls, and those assigned female at birth.
Antigoni’s inaugural summit included a showcase of femtech founders, a conversation with the Alberta Women’s Health Foundation, and a keynote address from Brittany Barreto, a US-based geneticist, author, and femtech founder. Barreto also owns the boutique research consultancy, FemHealth Insights, which has carried out extensive research into the global femtech industry.
Barreto’s research underscores how the femtech sector has grown dramatically over the last decade. FemHealth Insight now maintains a database of more than 1,700 femtech startups in operation worldwide, up from 1,400 just a few years ago. And while 85 percent of those startups are women-founded, they often receive significantly less investment dollars than their male counterparts, even if they’re closing more deals.
It was that research that underpinned the summit’s closing panel: a discussion with Canadian VCs on how femtech startup founders can approach raising capital and what can be done to rebalance the investment equation.
The same, but different
Courtney Dragani, the chief growth officer with The51, a VC firm that invests in women-led companies, spoke to what fund managers are looking for when they consider femtech as a potential investment.
“What we look for in femtech isn’t different from any other company in that we want some demonstration that the problem is sizable enough, and that people are willing to pay for it,” Dragani said.
Problems abound in women’s health, according to Barreto, who said that in her home country of the US, less than one percent of pharmaceutical R&D funding goes toward women’s health discoveries. In Canada, men’s bodies have been the default model for scientific and medical study; A Canadian Institutes of Health Research report shows that, as recently as 2010, fewer than 25 percent of health researchers accounted for sex in their studies. The same report says that gender was almost entirely ignored.
Those differences have led to poorer outcomes for women, who more commonly experience adverse side effects of drugs, or late and under-diagnosed illnesses. That, according to Barreto, is not only harmful to women, but to business, too.
RELATED: For Canadian femtech, women’s autonomy is part of the business model
“If you’re an investor, a stockholder investing in pharmaceutical companies that aren’t looking at female-specific data, that is a risk to your business,” Barreto said during her keynote address.
As robust as the problem set is, the market for its solutions is equally large. Consultancy firm McKinsey estimated that addressing those gaps could spur $1 trillion in global GDP development by 2040.
“We know there’s a significant white space where women are driving really compelling innovation, and it has been undercapitalized,” Dragani said. “It has the capability to outperform and we’re trying to find what those pockets are to put our capital into.”
Fixing the funding problem
Femtech Connect’s investor panel didn’t argue with the notion that VC dollars are disproportionately heading to male-founded businesses, but their solution had more to do with activating women in venture capital than any one piece of individual advice for founders looking to pitch fund managers.
“We … need to see more change in terms of who has the authority to make investment decisions,” Dragani said, noting that less than 15 percent of VC general partners in Canada are women. “It’s mostly men making the investment decisions, but once you shift those numbers to 30, 40 percent of women in those decision-making rooms, then we see notable differences in terms of where capital flows.”
That sentiment was echoed by Kristina Milke, a general partner with Sprout Fund, a Western Canadian firm investing in B2B companies. Milke said she believes more private investment from women would help move the needle.
“Women putting their money into this asset class would be super helpful. There are a lot of women who manage their household’s money and are unclear on where to put it,” she said. “There’s some education opportunities that could really help educate women with capital to think about where they would like to put their money.”
“Women are so often asked about where they want to donate, but they are rarely asked about where they want to invest,” Dragani added. “Those don’t need to be two separate lenses. You can drive change forward that’s very meaningful by putting your capital at risk rather than just giving it away.” 
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of Jesse Cole for BetaKit.

articles.title: EDA’s Future Is Evidence-Driven Automation
articles.text:
AI may accelerate semiconductor design, but users still need formal proof, semantic continuity, and auditable workflows to trust automation.
Key Takeaways:
AI is arriving in EDA at a time when engineers can no longer depend on brute-force scaling for performance and power improvements, and when the gaps created by disconnected point tools are becoming increasingly time-consuming to fill.
As designs expand to tens of billions of transistors and incorporate chiplets in multi-die assemblies, the hardest problems increasingly sit between tools — preserving intent, managing interdependencies, and identifying potential failures before they reach tapeout. At advanced nodes, where design costs can reach hundreds of millions of dollars and a single respin can threaten an entire program, AI’s real value will depend on whether it can accelerate various steps in the design flow while organizing and interpreting the data needed to trust the results.
The balance is between reliability and practicality. The global shortage of skilled engineers has not gone away. But it has made workflow automation more attractive, provided it can either improve the productivity of human engineers or achieve comparable results.
“Every customer is saying, ‘Give me the ability to shrink my time to results by at least 2×,’” said Ankur Gupta, executive vice president and head of EDA IC software at Siemens EDA. “Demand is pushing EDA toward a new operating model built on faster engines, smarter execution, and trusted outcomes. Acceleration may come from GPUs, machine learning, or reinforcement learning, but the larger goal is to shorten design cycles without losing confidence in the result.”
Efficiency also matters at the agent layer. Allowing any agent to call any tool may be flexible, but it can be expensive and inefficient if the underlying interfaces are poorly written. The goal is to do more of that integration work in advance so customers can either use a vendor’s agents or their own without paying unnecessary token and orchestration costs.
The economics of AI are becoming increasingly important as engineers incorporate it at various places in the design process.
“If I spend more money on tokens than a human would cost, then it doesn’t make sense,” said Thomas Andersen, vice president of the AI Excellence Group at Synopsys. “Agentic AI is useful only when it reduces the cost and complexity of production workflows. An agentic loop can perform sequences of tasks that an expert would otherwise handle manually, from automating repetitive steps to coordinating work across tools. Everybody wants to automate their workflows. They want agentic automation because that’s their way to productivity, to faster tape-out cycles, cutting costs, everything.”
The hard part isn’t dropping a tool. It’s integrating agents into real customers’ design flows.
Current challenges
Semiconductor design is inherently a multi-tool process, spanning architecture, IP configuration, integration, verification, implementation, and sign-off. The challenge is not simply moving data from one tool to another, but preserving the design intent, assumptions, and engineering context behind that data. “At the system level, where connectivity, address maps, performance constraints, and security requirements must remain consistent across many IP blocks and, increasingly, across multiple dies, engineers often serve as the integration layer,” explained Andy Nightingale, vice president of product management and marketing at Arteris.
That becomes increasingly difficult as systems grow in complexity. “The same architectural intent may be represented differently across integration, performance analysis, verification, and implementation environments,” Nightingale said. “If those representations diverge, the result can be additional verification cycles, manual rework, and late discovery of system-level issues. Better optimization between tools therefore needs to provide semantic continuity across the design flow, not simply file-format interoperability.”
Still, AI’s real impact on EDA will be less about sign-off and more about streamlining the peripheral process and data-management work around the flow. “There’s as much value there now as in the core simulators and layout tools, and that’s where AI can help you get things done much faster,” said Chris Mueth, new opportunities business manager at Keysight EDA.
Chip design is essentially a relay race involving dozens of specialized tools, including architectural exploration, RTL, lint, clock-domain crossing, formal, simulation, synthesis, place-and-route, timing and power sign-off, physical verification, equivalence checking, DFT, and post-silicon correlation.
“Each was written by a different vendor, against a different data model, with different assumptions about what ‘done’ means,” said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise. “The relay is where most of the pain lives. As the Agentic Electronic Design Automation: A Handoff Perspective survey puts it, EDA is ‘inherently multi-stage and handoff-heavy,’ and every artifact crosses tool, session, and organizational boundaries before signoff. Each transfer is a chance to lose information, silently reinterpret intent, or push a decision that was locally optimal in one tool into a globally suboptimal position downstream.”
Darbari groups the core workflow challenges into a few recurring failure modes:
That is why the next phase of AI in EDA is shifting from optimizing individual tools to coordinating the people, engines, and domain knowledge that sit between them.
Solaiman Rahim, chief product officer at ChipAgents, said tool-level AI has already improved individual engines, but the larger opportunity is coordinating the dependencies between tools and people. A DFT engineer, for example, may complete insertion correctly but still need timing analysis, expert interpretation, and another round of fixes before the work is usable. Each handoff can add days. “If you have a DFT agent handling DFT insertion and a timing agent that runs timing and debugs timing, these two agents can work together to speed up the process,” Rahim said. “Instead of taking weeks, it can take potentially just hours.”
That speedup requires more than scripts. Workflows need access to methodology, design knowledge, and context accumulated across teams. Rahim described an ontology layer that can capture why expert engineers avoid certain cells, choose particular constraints, or debug recurring failures, then make that know-how available to less experienced users and to coordinated AI workflows.
The same need for workflow-level coordination shows up outside the core digital flow, particularly where physical analysis depends on moving design data, assumptions, and results across multiple engineering domains. Satish Radhakrishnan, head of go-to-market for semiconductor and electronics at Vinci, said physics-based analysis faces the same workflow problem. Specialized tools may work well on their own, but model preparation, data movement, specialist handoffs, and result interpretation still slow the loop. By the time the analysis returns, the design may already have changed.
The problem grows as chips, packages, and systems become more tightly coupled. A chip-level change can affect package and board temperatures, mechanical stress, warpage, and reliability, none of which respects the boundary between tools or teams.
Radhakrishnan said much of the delay occurs before a solver starts. Engineers still clean geometry, create meshes, apply materials and boundary conditions, and hand results between design and simulation specialists. That process may support scheduled analysis, but it cannot provide reliable feedback each time a design changes. The goal, he said, is to move from isolated simulation checkpoints to continuous physics reasoning inside the design workflow.
Where EDA workflows are headed
ChipAgent’s Rahim predicts that the next layer of AI assistance will depend on understanding design intent, not just parsing cells and wires. “In SoC debug, for example, an AI system that understands the instruction being executed, the memory operation involved, and the relevant cycles in a waveform can help narrow a failure the way an expert designer would. The value comes from pairing intent recognition with an intelligence layer that can take action across the workflow.”
As part of this, requirements management is essential. “Today’s AI still has room for error, so you don’t let it own specifications or sign-off,” said Keysight’s Meuth. “You use it to accelerate the workflow around those decisions, not to make the decisions themselves.”
These safeguards are being implemented wherever AI is used. Paul Graykowski, director of product marketing at Cadence, pointed to one guardrail for AI-assisted testbench enhancement. Rather than allowing an agent to rewrite code unilaterally, the system surfaces the proposed refactoring for review. “The tool actually picks up those differences, and it will propose fixes,” Graykowski said. “It’s going to look at it and just say, ‘Okay, here’s the refactoring I’m proposing. Take a look at it. Do you approve?'”
That same approval model can support more autonomous regression repair, as long as the changes remain isolated until an engineer accepts them. Graykowski said one customer wanted an agent to analyze failures, make candidate fixes, rerun the regression, and return with a sandboxed result: “I’ve created a snapshot of your code, I’ve gone off, and I’ve worked on it in this sandbox. Here are the changes I’ve made. Do you approve these changes now?”
Darbari sees three emerging ways AI can reduce cross-tool friction, ranging from near-term optimization to deeper infrastructure changes. But he draws a sharp distinction between automation that preserves context and automation that simply adds another agent to the relay.
For formal verification, AI is most valuable when handoff loss is high. “LLMs can extract properties, suggest assertions, propose abstractions, and triage proofs. However, AI outputs must be independently verified, as generated assertions are hypotheses, not proof. Only a completed proof against a correct property counts as evidence. A prompt is not proof,” Darbari said.
Cadence’s Graykowski noted that kind of checked assistance could also lower the barrier to formal verification for teams without deep formal expertise. If engineers can define intent or provide a specification, an agent can help generate candidate properties and check code before it reaches simulation or a formal engine such as Jasper. The point is not to replace formal expertise, but to move more designs toward machine-checkable evidence earlier in the flow.
Further, Darbari observed that single-tool AI features are becoming table stakes. “The next competitive frontier is between tools — agentic orchestration, standardized data models, and the ability to move constraints, waivers, and evidence across tool boundaries without loss. The FluxBench evaluation of AI agents attempting end-to-end RTL-to-GDSII is a sobering reminder that the seams are still hard. The problem is not the AI. It is the lack of a shared semantic substrate for the AI to reason over.”
The need for a shared semantic substrate is where orchestration becomes more than automation. The agent has to understand not only which tool to call next, but what each result means in the larger system context.
AI can provide an intelligent orchestration layer across EDA tools. “Rather than requiring an engineer to manually inspect every result and determine the next action, an AI agent can correlate information from multiple tools, understand the wider system context, and recommend or execute the appropriate next step,” Arteris’ Nightingale said. “For example, it could identify a system-level performance issue, relate that issue to an architectural or configuration decision, make a controlled change, and rerun the relevant analysis to determine whether the result has improved.”
A fundamental shift in AI’s evolution involves moving from operating inside individual tools to operating between tools. Standardized interfaces can make EDA capabilities accessible to agents, but tool access alone is not enough.
“AI also needs domain-specific context, a consistent representation of design intent, controlled permissions, and measurable results against which its actions can be checked. In this model, AI provides reasoning and orchestration while established EDA engines continue to provide deterministic analysis and verification,” Nightingale explained.
Rahim expects compute to keep moving up the stack, first from tools to workflows, and eventually from workflows into chip-design-specific models. Today’s frontier models are not yet specialized, cost-effective, or physically aware enough to generate fully verified, PPA-optimized RTL, analog layouts, advanced packaging, or netlists on demand. But he believes that capability will improve as models absorb more workflow knowledge and domain context. “We are confident we can tackle the problem because our customers are pulling us. Semiconductors are becoming a commodity. The number of projects they have to do, the number of layouts, and the analog experts they have available no longer scale. Because of that, our customers need a solution in that space, and they are looking for a partner to work with. They are willing to share a lot of that layout knowledge for us to train on.”
Additionally, Vinci’s Radhakrishnan said that AI can remove repetitive work around physics analysis by preparing inputs, invoking the right tools, carrying results forward, and comparing alternatives within engineer-defined boundaries. But the agent is only as useful as the analysis beneath it. If simulation still requires hours of manual setup and days to run, an AI front end does not solve the bottleneck. Agentic workflows become useful when the underlying analysis is fast, automated, deterministic, and production-scale.
In Vinci’s case, the approach is to ingest native design files and pair pretrained physics models with GPU-native numerical physics kernels, producing solver-accurate results without human meshing or customer-specific training data. Radhakrishnan said the point is not probabilistic simulation-by-chatbot, but repeatable physics results that can be used while the design is still changing.
Many companies are now using agentic AI or other types of AI to enhance workflows or optimize tools in the EDA process, as well as for other reasons. Mo Faisal, founder and CEO of Movellus, sees this as an advantage for new companies. “They’re starting from scratch, and I’m a little jealous of companies born in the last month. They don’t have the baggage, at least in Silicon Valley. The most common use I’ve seen is automatic customer ticket triage, customer success, and customer support. You put in the documentation and all of your context. When a customer ticket comes in, it is automatically processed, though there’s still a human in the loop. That workflow is probably the earliest in terms of benefiting from agentic AI first.”
From a product development point of view, agentic AI is being used to create product definition specs and do quick prototyping. “Product management is blurring with engineering,” Faisal observed. “Design is product management and engineering, so the workflow changes are happening there for the open-minded teams,” Faisal noted. “In other areas like legal and accounting, etc., that’s low-hanging fruit, but bringing agentic AI into complex engineering workflow- that’s the really interesting part here. It’s definitely happening. People have libraries of skill files now, so with whatever they’re doing for their workflow, they have a bunch of skill files that are skilled in a certain step; then models are called in as they’re processing that. Yet, while this is true in Silicon Valley, if you go somewhere else, it’s not happening yet.”
Raising the abstraction
As the industry gains experience with AI, EDA workflows are likely to become increasingly intent-driven. “Rather than directly operating every tool and manually translating information between different environments, engineers will increasingly be able to specify objectives such as performance targets, connectivity requirements, security policies, or implementation constraints,” Nightingale said. “AI agents can then help determine which analyses and tools are required to meet those objectives and coordinate the necessary iterations across the design flow.”
This will make verification even more important. As agents are trusted to make larger changes and run longer workflows, every action will need an observable, verifiable outcome. “The most effective future EDA environments are therefore likely to combine AI-driven exploration and orchestration with deterministic engineering tools that continuously provide ground truth. The objective is not autonomous chip design for its own sake, but to reduce repetitive tool interactions and manual translation so engineers can spend more time making architectural and system-level decisions,” he said.
Radhakrishnan said the first challenge is to remove discrete bottlenecks, such as model preparation, analysis setup, and result comparison. Over time, those steps can become part of connected design loops in which an agent proposes a change, initiates the right physics analysis, checks the result against requirements, and either explores another option or sends the design to an engineer for review.
That would enable engineering teams to consider many more ideas. In fact, engineers who now test a handful of options may be able to examine hundreds or thousands, turning design exploration from a scheduled event into an iterative, more creative part of daily engineering work. But Radhakrishnan noted that the boundary between automation and human judgment will still matter. Early exploration may tolerate more autonomy, but validation and signoff require traceability, reproducibility, and deterministic results.
The longer-term opportunity is a design environment where AI agents coordinate specialized tools while deterministic physics keeps pace with the ideas engineers generate. In that model, physical behavior is evaluated throughout the flow, not only at scheduled checkpoints.
Axiomise’s Darbari pointed to visible shifts, each of which he expects to accelerate over the next two to three years. “The first shift is from tool-level AI to flow-level evidence. The first generation of AI in EDA sold productivity. The second will be judged on evidence. A signoff report that says, ‘The AI copilot converged the design in 40% less time,’ is interesting to a project manager. A signoff report that says ‘these properties are proven, these are bounded, these are AI-suggested and not yet checked, here is the reproducibility record,’ is what a safety, security, or automotive customer will accept. The current infatuation with autonomy will give way to an insistence on auditability. The second shift is occurring from simulation confidence to proof-backed signoff. The shift I care about most is from ‘we ran a lot of simulation, and everything looked green’ to ‘we can point at machine-checkable evidence for the properties that matter, and AI helped us get there faster.’ AI-assisted property extraction, agentic coverage closure, and LLM-driven abstraction discovery are real accelerators, but their output has to land on a formal engine that produces deterministic proof, or the confidence is theater. Apple’s Hilbert system, which wraps informal LLM reasoning around Lean 4, is the clearest public example of the architecture that will win. AI for exploration. Formal for correctness closure.”
Another wrinkle is that AI silicon splits into two verification and signoff regimes. “Training hardware lives or dies on distributed progress, collective operations, numerically valid reductions, and silent-data-corruption resilience across large clusters,” Darbari added. “Inference hardware, especially decode-heavy serving, lives on KV-cache ownership, scheduling, isolation, fairness, and tail latency. The cross-tool optimizations that matter for a training accelerator don’t matter for an inference tile. The AI-in-EDA story will fragment along the same lines. AI will not remove the need for handoffs. A boundary will always exist between architectural intent and implementation, between design and verification, and between pre-silicon proof and post-silicon behavior. AI can compress the reconciliation tax at each boundary and give engineers more time for the questions only humans can answer. Use AI for speed. Use formal for truth. Treat the boundaries between tools as places to accumulate evidence, not places to lose it.”
That shift from tool-level automation to flow-level evidence also changes what EDA companies and engineering teams have to organize around.
Organizational changes required
Tool vendors face the same organizational challenge as their customers. Agents built inside individual product groups can recreate the silos they are supposed to remove. Synopsys’ Andersen said the shift has to be guided from the top, not left entirely to bottom-up experimentation. “Every product team tends to say, ‘I’m going to build an agent in my domain, but we have to look at the whole flow.”
That matters because agentic EDA will fail if it simply adds another layer of locally optimized automation. To reduce handoff loss, organizations need shared ownership of the end-to-end flow, common data and permission models, and metrics that measure whether agents improve engineering outcomes rather than merely execute more steps.
Rahim expects workflows to advance over the next six months, especially in root-cause analysis, verification, timing closure, physical design, analog, and advanced packaging. But he cautioned that complex, fully optimized designs remain beyond current frontier models. The likely path, he said, is gradual, with specialized workflows becoming more capable, workflow knowledge moving into model layers, and chip-design models becoming more physically aware through collaboration with customers and foundries.
Graykowski succinctly framed where AI belongs in this flow: “We’re leveraging these tools as assistants, not replacements. You have to guide it. They’re the junior engineer. You’re the senior engineer.”
That may be the most practical way to think about AI’s role in EDA. It will not eliminate the boundaries between specification, implementation, verification, signoff, packaging, and post-silicon learning. Nor will it make probabilistic answers acceptable where deterministic proof is required. Its value will come from what happens at those boundaries: whether agents can carry intent, assumptions, constraints, results, and proof across the flow without losing meaning. If they can, evidence-driven automation becomes more than a productivity story. It becomes the foundation for EDA workflows that execute faster, are easier to audit, and are safer to trust.

articles.title: Ghana’s Hyphine is a client review and approval platform for creative professionals - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ghanaian startup Hyphine has built a client review and approval platform for freelancers, creative teams, and agencies, which takes a piece of work from first draft to final approval in one link.
Founded earlier this year by Salih Abdulrahman, a graphic designer and creative professional, Hyphine is a visual collaboration platform and workspace that consolidates client reviews, design iterations, and feedback loops into a single shared link to eliminate fragmented communication across emails or messaging apps.
The idea came from a problem Abdulrahman experienced firsthand.
“Working with creative teams and clients, I repeatedly saw the same pattern – creating the design wasn’t always the difficult part. The friction came afterwards, sending work, collecting feedback, understanding what the client meant, keeping track of revisions, finding the right version, and eventually getting a clear approval,” he told Disrupt Africa.
Over time, it became clear that the industry had plenty of tools for creating and managing work, but the space between “here’s the work” and “approved” was still unnecessarily fragmented.
That became the starting point for Hyphine.
“Today, the creative process often breaks down after the work is created. A designer might send a file through WhatsApp or email, share a Google Drive folder, receive feedback in a mix of messages and screenshots, make revisions, send another version, and repeat the cycle several times. Feedback becomes scattered. Context gets lost. Designers have to figure out which version a client is referring to, what exactly needs to change, and whether a particular comment has already been addressed,” Abdulrahman said.
“Hyphine brings that entire review cycle into one place. At its simplest, Hyphine gives creative professionals one link to take a piece of work from first draft to final approval.”
A creative uploads their work and shares a single link with the client. The client can open it without creating an account, comment directly on the work, pin feedback to specific areas, annotate what they want changed, respond to conversations, and approve the final version.
Behind that experience, Hyphine keeps the versions and feedback connected.
“We’re also building AI into the workflow to help turn unstructured client feedback into clearer, actionable revision lists, summarise conversations, identify outstanding changes, and make it easier for teams to understand what needs to happen next,” said Abdulrahman.
“The bigger idea is simple. Creative teams shouldn’t lose time managing the communication around their work. They should be able to focus on the work itself.”
The bootstrapped startup has already built up a reasonable user base, but Abdulrahman said it is being intentional about how it measures progress.
“At this point, we don’t want to confuse sign-ups with product-market fit,” he said. “For us, the strongest validation won’t simply be a growing registration number. It will be seeing a designer or agency send their second, third, and tenth client review through Hyphine because it has become easier than the workflow they were using before.”
Hyphine is being built in Ghana, with a broader African market in mind.
“We’re particularly interested in the growing ecosystem of African freelancers, studios, agencies, and independent creative professionals who increasingly work with clients across borders and timezones,” Abdulrahman said.
“But the problem we’re solving isn’t unique to Africa. Whether you’re a small design studio in Accra, a branding agency in Lagos, or a creative team working with clients in London or New York, the underlying problem is familiar. Our ambition is therefore global.”

articles.title: Tech Guide goes eyes-on with the new Meta VR Glasses - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Tech Guide got the chance to go eyes-on with the new Meta VR Glasses which was announced by Mark Zuckerberg at Meta Connect 2026 at the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park.
The Meta VR Glasses go on sale in the US Spring 2027 (March or April) for $US1,299.99.
The straight conversion to Australian dollars puts it at $1,834. We’re hoping it to be priced at $1,999.
Before we tried the Meta VR Glasses our prescription glasses were scanned before corresponding magnetic lens inserts added to make the experience sharp and clear.
The first thing you notice is just how small and light the device is and how light it feels on your face.
This makes it even more accessible as does the more affordable price which is less than a third of that of its nearest competitor, the Apple Vision Pro.
The Meta VR glasses have no straps and require no major adjustments.
You just put them on as easily as a pair of glasses and you’re ready to go.
The glasses are attached with an optical cable to what Meta calls a puck which looks like a power bank and is slightly smaller than a smartphone.
The puck contains the battery, along with storage and the processor for the glasses.
Image quality was stunning as we were taken through a demo that showed us everything from 3D movies to apps, games and sports.
We also experienced ESPN Immersive Sports which put us courtside at an NBA match with a 180° view, which made us feel like we were there.
We also got a chance to experience the VR-enhanced version of an Avengers film which added detail and light and content outside of the main frame of the movie, which immersed us even further into the action.
And with the speakers built into the arms of the glasses, the audio was also loud and clear.
It was also easy to navigate the system with a simple pinch gesture of your thumb and forefinger.
And to scroll you simply make a fist and rub your thumb on your forefinger.
It was surprisingly responsive and easy to navigate the entire system.
What was impressive was the ability to create a workspace through the Meta VR Glasses.
We were able to place a virtual keyboard and trackpad on the table in front of us and type just as freely as if we were using a physical keyboard – it was incredibly responsive and accurate.
We also got a chance to play a game without a controller anywhere in sight.
The game was Beat Saber. It was a music game like Guitar Hero, where you had to hit various symbols with your left, right, or both hands as the song played over the action.
It was smooth as silk and got us up out of our chair so it also gave us a bit of exercise at the same time.
There will no doubt be the inevitable comparison with Apple’s Vision Pro because there are a few similarities including the controller-free operation.
In fact one of the gestures to select is identical to that put forward by Apple when it released the Apple Vision Pro in 2024.
Even the ability to select apps and buttons just by looking at it was also a major feature of Apple’s mixed reality product.
But one area where Meta was no doubt happy to undercut Apple was the price.
In Australia the Apple Vision Pro is priced from $6,299. If Meta VR is priced as we hoped at $1,999 it will be less than a third of the price.
The Meta VR will not be released until around March or April in 2027 and it is sure to attract customers to the platform and a whole new way of experiencing their content at a more affordable price.
* Stephen Fenech travelled to the US as a guest of Meta.

articles.title: Ema raises $77M in funding to deploy AI employees across enterprise HR, IT and finance departments - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Ema raises $77M in funding to deploy AI employees across enterprise HR, IT and finance departments
Agentic artificial intelligence employee startup Ema Unlimited Inc. is prepping for a massive expansion of its autonomous workers in the enterprise after raising $77 million in funding today.
The Series B round was led by Creagis and saw the participation of existing backers including Accel, S32 and Posus, which each returned with a substantially larger investment, the company said. Ema said it will use the funds to expand and accelerate the development of its agentic employees, which help to automate business operations across human resources, information technology and finance.
The startup has built a number of AI agents designed to act like “autonomous AI employees.” Unlike traditional generative AI chatbots, its agents are designed not to answer questions but to take actions upon request and execute complex tasks within enterprise software systems.
Once given a task to complete, they’ll set about planning how to do it, before executing within the applications and systems that companies already use to conduct their business. They’re also designed to check their own work and notify their human overseers when they’re needed to approve sensitive actions.
Ema says it has taken a product-led approach to agentic AI development in order to make deployments faster and simpler for organizations. With its platform, customers can implement prebuilt AI employees in a specific area, such as HR or finance, without having to lean on expensive professional services or design their own governance and control frameworks first. They can also use its tools and frameworks to design their own, specialized employees.
It’s a more streamlined model for agentic AI adoption, and the startup says this approach has enabled it to generate real traction at a time when many enterprise AI projects have stalled at the testing and pilot phase. In the last two years, Ema has grown its revenue by more than 50 times, off an undisclosed base, and the average customer has more than doubled its spending on its AI workers in the last year by expanding initial deployments.
Co-founder and Chief Executive Surojit Chatterjee told SiliconANGLE that this model has paid off, because enterprises don’t want to deal with the hassles of integrating new software and tools. All they want to do is get work done, and providing a qualified and deployment-ready digital employee is the best way to do that.
“Our customers are not running experiments,” he stressed. “They are running their HR, IT and finance operations on AI employees at a scale of millions of interactions per year. This round will let us bring that to many more enterprises who’re still stuck in the pilot stage.”
Chatterjee’s claims are backed up by the experiences of several large enterprises that have already embraced its AI employees. They include the consulting firm Wipro Ltd., which has deployed an Ema-powered AI assistant for more than 240,000 employees spread across 65 countries. Those AI assistants handle around 2.9 million queries per year across approximately 100 automated workflows, leading to a 50% reduction in the number of IT support tickets.
Hitachi Ltd. is another customer. When it started out with Ema’s AI employees, it was able to move from concept to full production in less than four weeks, integrating them with more than 20 enterprise systems. Support ticket volumes are down 30%, while employees have increased their efficiency by 70%, Ema said.
Creagis Managing Partner and Chief Investment Officer Prakash Parthasarathy said Ema is one of only a handful of agentic AI companies he has seen that can actually deliver at enterprise scale. “Ema stands apart, and its platform already supports millions of employee interactions at some of the world’s largest organizations,” he said.
Ema said it will use the cash from today’s round to expand its go-to-market teams, hire more executive leaders and further the development of its AI employees to enhance their capabilities.

articles.title: OT Security Guidance: NIST Drafts Updated Guide, CISA/FBI Advise on ICS Integrators
articles.text:
NIST has published a draft update to its operational technology security guide, and CISA and the FBI have issued a fact sheet on the risks of working with third-party ICS integrators.
NIST seeks comment on revised OT guide
NIST this week released a draft of Special Publication 800-82 Revision 4, titled Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security. Public comments are due by November 30, 2026. The document covers how to secure OT while accounting for the performance, reliability and safety demands specific to these systems.
The revision expands the guide’s sector coverage to include building automation, water and wastewater systems, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and the convergence of industrial IoT and cloud.
The guide is now organized around NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, and the former risk management section has been reorganized to focus on the framework’s Govern function.
NIST also expanded its guidance on implementing OT security controls, including asset management and network monitoring and detection.
The updated version also includes security architecture guidelines for protecting system management functions and applying zero trust principles.
CISA and FBI urge scrutiny of ICS integrators
CISA and the FBI published the fact sheet for critical infrastructure owners and operators that work with third-party industrial control system (ICS) integrators. The agencies urge caution when giving integrators high levels of access or control over industrial processes.
They recommend granting users, processes and systems “only the minimum access necessary to perform their assigned tasks, and no more.” Failing to apply the principle of least privilege could expose operators to malicious cyber actors, the agencies say.
The document cites FBI technical analysis of an intrusion at a US industrial automation solutions company. Between March and April 2025, malicious foreign cyber actors gained access to the company’s network. The company provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming to customers that included power utilities and transportation companies.
During the intrusion, foreign actors searched for SCADA and customer records and staged nine archive files containing 800 network schematics, device configurations, and customer details that could enable downstream disruptive attacks.
The agencies recommend that operators include cybersecurity and supply chain requirements in contracts and service agreements, covering areas such as data storage locations, remote access, and patch management.
They also advise working with integrators to find out where devices are hosted and to reduce exposure, including by disconnecting devices from the public-facing internet. Operators should monitor and log remote access and, where possible, use on-demand remote access.
