articles.title: China puts AI compute into orbit with Supercomputing-1 satellite — onboard processing aims to cut Earth-observation data processing from hours to minutes
articles.text:
China puts AI compute into orbit with Supercomputing-1 satellite — onboard processing aims to cut Earth-observation data processing from hours to minutes
But it's a far cry from an orbital data center.
China has launched nine satellites — including its first integrated “rocket and satellite” AI computing project — as part of its push to put AI computing in orbit. According to a Digitimes report, the Kinetica 1 Y18 rocket, operated by Chinese commercial launch provider CAS Space, lifted off on September 20, carrying the nine satellites to their planned orbits.
The payload of greatest interest is the “Supercomputing-1” satellite, developed by Chinese AI computing infrastructure company S-AIDC. Also known as the S-AIDC-1, the satellite is designed to capture and process Earth-observation data in orbit instead of sending data back to terrestrial data centers. Keeping the processing local is meant to cut cross-regional data processing times from hours to minutes. The satellite features both a high-res optical payload and the image-processing AI computer.
According to Digitimes, the launch highlights China's efforts to develop orbital computing as part of a “broader integrated computing network.” In early June, the Chinese government approved the Space Computing Industry Innovation Center, which aims to bring together rocket and satellite manufacturers, semiconductor fabs, and AI tech companies to build a space computing network. A couple of factors are driving this spike in the development of off-planet computing, foremost among them being the AI boom.
The demand for artificial intelligence has spurred the construction of numerous data centers to house AI accelerators. These data centers, some of which can house hundreds of thousands of accelerators, consume unprecedented amounts of electricity, placing significant strain on the grid. This, along with land use, water consumption for cooling, and noise, has fueled growing anti-data sentiment, with local residents blocking $68 billion worth of new data center projects in Q2 2026.
Despite numerous economic and practical challenges, space might offer an alternative with unlimited area, access to solar power, constant cold conditions, and a dead-quiet vacuum. These advantages have made orbital computing a serious topic of discussion. SpaceX is leading the charge with the AI1 satellite, a proposed orbital data center that will deliver 150 kW of peak compute power. The company aims to achieve 1 GW per year of space AI compute by 2027 and has begun constructing the 11-million-square-foot Gigasat facility that would manufacture the 6,000 satellites required to meet this goal.
Beyond the large-scale serving of AI models, putting edge compute capacity in space is already useful for a range of applications. Earth-observation satellites can process images onboard to identify wildfires, storms, floods, ships, or other objects of interest, sending only the useful results back to Earth instead of dumping enormous amounts of raw data to ground stations. The same approach can speed up weather monitoring, disaster response, communications, and even the management of satellite constellations, where spacecraft could make more decisions independently rather than waiting for instructions from Earth.
The launch of a single satellite with edge AI capabilities on board is a far cry from an entire orbital data center, but China's approach could prove to be a more practical and immediate application for advanced computing capabilities in orbit.

articles.title: Windows-Probleme lösen, bevor sie auftauchen: Mit diesen Tools repariert sich dein PC selbst
articles.text:
Ohne Fremdsoftware: So bringst du deinem Windows-PC bei, sich automatisch zu reparieren
Wer Windows regelmäßig nutzt, wird zwangsweise irgendwann auf kleinere und größere Probleme stoßen. Manche davon wurden durch Update-Fehler von Microsoft versehentlich in das Betriebssystem integriert, andere ergeben sich eher durch die Aktionen der User:innen selbst. Egal, um welche Fehler es sich handelt: Sobald sie sichtbar werden, gehen sie Windows-User:innen auf die Nerven.
Doch tatsächlich muss es in vielen Fällen gar nicht so weit kommen. Du kannst deinen Windows-PC regelmäßig Aufgaben durchführen lassen, die die Probleme frühzeitig sichtbar und behebbar machen. Dafür benötigst du kein tiefgreifendes Programmierwissen oder zusätzliche Software von Drittanbieter:innen, wie How to Geek zeigt. Windows hat die notwendigen Tools alle schon an Bord.
Die Grundlage: Windows-Aufgaben planen
Zunächst braucht es ein Tool, das in regelmäßigen Abständen automatisch verschiedene Aufgaben anstoßen kann, mit denen Windows sich selbst auf Fehler überprüft. Das Windows-Programm heißt „Aufgabenplanung“ und kann direkt über die Suchfunktion im Startmenü geöffnet werden. Die Optionen, die die Aufgabenplanung bietet, sind leicht verständlich, können aber mächtige Automatisierungen in Windows auslösen.
Wenn du eine geplante Aufgabe erstellst, musst du einen Namen dafür festlegen. Danach kannst du einen Trigger auswählen. Das kann etwa ein bestimmter Zeitpunkt oder der Systemstart sein. Im Anschluss legst du fest, welche Aktion immer dann ausgeführt werden soll, wenn der Trigger erkannt wird. In diesem Fall wirst du Windows mehrere Aufträge geben, Programme auszuführen, die das System auf Fehler prüfen und wenn möglich beheben.
Dazu können in der Windows-Aufgabenplanung auch noch Bedingungen eingefügt werden, unter denen die Automatisierung ausgelöst wird. Willst du etwa, dass dein Laptop die aufwendigen Aufgaben nur durchführt, wenn er mit einem Ladekabel an den Strom angeschlossen ist, kannst du das hier einstellen. Das verhindert, dass der Akku unnötig belastet wird, wenn du unterwegs bist.
Windows-Reparatur anstoßen
Die erste regelmäßige Aufgabe, die du Windows geben solltest, ist es, kaputte Dateien zu reparieren. Dafür gibt es den DISM-Befehl, der über die Kommandozeile ausgelöst werden kann. DISM kommt mit einigen Parametern daher, die verschiedene Bereiche des Systems abdecken. Im Aufgabenplaner legst du zunächst fest, dass diese Aufgabe einmal in der Woche gestartet werden soll. Am besten wählst du eine Zeit, in der der Computer zwar angeschaltet ist, du ihn aber nur für leichte Aufgaben benötigst. DISM kann unter Umständen etwas ressourcenintensiver sein.
Dann gibst du als Aktion ohne Anführungszeichen „DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth“ ein. Beim Bestätigen bietet dir Windows direkt an, dass es sich um einen DISM-Befehl mit mehreren Parametern handelt und fragt, ob dieser entsprechend so umgesetzt werden soll. Der erste Befehl zielt darauf ab, Fehler zum Vorschein zu bringen, die vom System schon im Hintergrund erkannt wurden. Erstelle dann einen zweiten Befehl mit „DISM /ScanHealth“, um einen Scan von Windows anzustoßen.
Zu guter Letzt fügst du als Aktion „DISM /RestoreHealth“ ein. Auch hier scannt Windows die eigenen Dateien noch einmal und versucht, sie im Anschluss zu reparieren. Stelle dafür sicher, dass du mit dem Internet verbunden bist. Denn Windows ersetzt etwaige beschädigte Dateien mit neuen aus offiziellen Microsoft-Quellen. Alternativ kannst du über den Parameter „/Source“ und einen Dateipfad auch ein Image von Windows als Quelle für die Reparaturdaten angeben. Die Aufgaben können ein paar Minuten beanspruchen. Sollten sie laufen, unterbrich sie nicht, da dadurch noch weitere Probleme auftreten könnten.
Windows-Systemdateien überprüfen
Auch bei der nächsten Aufgabe solltest du einen wöchentlichen Turnus festlegen, der immer dann greift, wenn du gerade leichte Aufgaben an deinem Windows-PC vornimmst. Denn das Überprüfen der Systemdateien ist nicht nur für die Festplatten, sondern auch für den Prozessor belastend. Auch hier kannst du als Aktion einen Kommandozeilenbefehl eingeben: „sfc /scannow“.
Beim Scan werden geschützte Systemdateien überprüft und eine Reparatur beschädigter Dateien angestoßen. Wird die Aufgabe abgeschlossen, zeigt der Systemscan an, ob beschädigte Dateien gefunden wurden und was mit ihnen passiert ist. Wer nicht direkt Änderungen am System vornehmen lassen will, sondern nur einen Bericht erhalten möchte, kann stattdessen auch „sfc /scannow /verifyonly“ eingeben.
Windows-Speicher bereinigen
Eine weitere Fehlerquelle sind die Festplatten, die in deinem PC verbaut sind. Läuft der Speicher voll, können dadurch vermehrt Fehler auftreten oder Windows ganz einfach Performance-Einbußen drohen. Deshalb ist es wichtig, gerade die Festplatte, auf der die Windows-Installation liegt, regelmäßig von unnötigem Datenmüll zu befreien. Und hier geben dir Windows und Microsoft gleich zwei Tools an die Hand.
Den Anfang macht die Speicheroptimierung. Das Tool bietet selbst eine Planfunktion. Du musst also keine Automatisierung durch die Aufgabenplanung anstoßen. Bei der Optimierung löscht das Tool nicht mehr benötigte Dateien, sobald die Festplatte vollläuft. Regelmäßige Scans nach solchen Dateien helfen, den Datenmüllberg klein zu halten.
Dazu gesellt sich die „Datenträgerbereinigung“, die du ebenfalls über die Suchleiste im Startmenü aufrufen kannst. Wähle darin die Festplatte aus, die bereinigt werden soll. Das Tool scannt sie und zeigt dir, wo es Potenzial gibt, Platz freizuschaufeln. So kannst du temporäre Dateien oder Miniaturansichten von Bildern und Videos löschen lassen. Darunter zeigt das Tool auch, wie viele Gigabyte dadurch freigeräumt werden.
Leider musst du das Tool händisch öffnen und einen Scan anstoßen. Stelle dir hierfür einen Reminder. Je nachdem, wie oft du deinen Windows-PC nutzt, reicht es meist auch aus, einen monatlichen Scan durchzuführen. Nutzt du ihn öfter, kannst du das Tool auch alle zwei Wochen nutzen. Probiere es einfach aus und schau, ob sich die Aufräumaktion nach dem ersten Zeitraum schon lohnt. Danach kannst du den Zeitabstand noch anpassen.

articles.title: Espectacular primer tráiler de 'Ray Gunn', la nueva película del director de 'Los Increíbles' para Netflix
articles.text:
Netflix tiene entre manos una nueva bomba en el cine de animación. La plataforma de streaming, de la mano de Skydance, acaba de estrenar el primer tráiler de Ray Gunn, la nueva película del mismísimo Brad Bird, el director de Los Increíbles o Ratatuille. El cineasta regresa por fin ocho años después de su último filme, Los Increíbles 2. Y lo hace con un proyecto que pinta espectacular.
Como vemos en el tráiler, Ray Gunn será una película de detectives y ciencia ficción. Ambientada en Metropia, una gigantesca ciudad de un futuro alternativo concebido en 1939, el detective privado Raymond Gunn se ve envuelto en un caso con alienígenas, un asesinato y una superestrella llamada Venus Nova.
La película lleva ya muchos años en desarrollo. De hecho, Brad Bird confesó que la idea de Ray Gunn se le ocurrió en su día tras ver el tráiler del telefilme Peter Gunn, del año 1989. Ya en los años 90 trató de hacerla realidad, pero finalmente no lo consiguió. Ahora, por fin ha podido llevarla a cabo e incluso aterrizará en cines pese a ser de Netflix.
Mira el tráiler de Ray Gunn
Durante un tiempo, Brad Bird se enfocó en el desarrollo de Los Increíbles 3 en Pixar. Sin embargo, pese a haber dirigido las dos primeras entregas, decidió hacerse a un lado para poder centrarse en Ray Gunn. Actualmente, Disney tiene totalmente en marcha la tercera entrega de la familia superheroica para 2028, pero el filme de Bird llegará antes a los cines.
En el reparto de Ray Gunn en su versión original destacan los nombres de Sam Rockwell y de Scarlett Johansson como Raymond Gunn y Venus Nova. Junto a ellos, Patton Oswalt, Kathryn Hunter, John Ratzenberger y Jamie Costa. La cinta será un neo-noir futurista y de ciencia ficción, con extraterrestres y toda clase de situaciones locas a las que su protagonista deberá hacer frente.
Ray Gunn se estrena en cines el 4 de diciembre y en Netflix el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
articles.text:
Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.
Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
Meta’s AI agent is arriving on its glasses alongside a wave of new accessibility, camera, and navigation features.
Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.
Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch.
The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”
A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. Starting later this month, users in the US and Canada will have an option to use their voice to ask for real-time cycling or public transit directions. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

articles.title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.
Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows.
Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.
YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation.
YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.
The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones.
Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes.
Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts.
The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to.
Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide.

articles.title: Aftermarket driver assist under federal probe following fatal crashes
articles.text:
Aftermarket devices that can boost or augment a vehicle’s native advanced driver assistance systems are the target of a new federal investigation this week. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation says it knows of five crashes in which drivers using devices from comma.ai crashed into stopped or slow-moving cars. Two of the crashes resulted in three deaths, and 11 people were injured in four of the five crashes, some seriously.
Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz, who rose to prominence at the start of the last decade by jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations. In 2015, Hotz turned his attention to partially automated driver assists, which were gaining attention following Tesla’s exploits with its Autopilot system. Hotz first modified his own Acura to give it a more advanced driver assist that let him take his hands off the wheel, with the goal of selling his system to Tesla and replacing Mobileye as the company’s supplier.
(Mobileye dropped Tesla as a customer the following year after becoming unhappy with the way the car company was using Mobileye products in unintended ways.)
Comma’s first attempts to sell devices that owners could plug into their cars’ ODB port evaporated once NHTSA began asking questions in 2016. Instead, Comma decided to post its openpilot software, as well as its plans for hardware, to GitHub, allowing anyone to make the devices themselves. At first, the Comma Neo and OpenPilot supported a single Acura and single Honda model, but by 2020, the company’s software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system.

articles.title: Smarter Buildings, Safer Occupants: Intelligence Meets Privacy - EE Times
articles.text:
Personal safety and security allow no compromise. From access control and video surveillance to smoke and fire alarms, HVAC, and lighting, modern building automation systems are designed to optimize energy efficiency while safeguarding the health, safety, and security of occupants.
In this Special Report, we explore how ambient light harvesting is expanding into buildings and how advanced sensors and AI-driven IoT solutions enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and faster emergency response—without compromising individual privacy.
What happens when sensors become ubiquitous? Can buildings harvest enough ambient energy to power their own sensors? Can buildings use light not just to illuminate spaces but also to power IoT devices, day and night? How can cameras improve safety without identifying individuals? Where should the intelligence reside: at the edge or in the cloud? How can increasingly connected building systems integrate without creating new security risks?
To answer these questions, this Special Report draws on interviews with companies such as Axis Communications, e-peas, Infineon Technologies, and Pimloc, as well as discussions with professors from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, the Laboratory for Future Interdisciplinary Research of Science and Technology at the Institute of Science Tokyo, and the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar. It also features contributions from Wireless Logic and Insight SiP.
Ambient IoT: From Battery-Free Promise to Mass-Market Reality
By Rebecca Pool
Surging investment, maturing tech, and emerging standards are pushing ambient IoT toward mainstream deployment.
Digital Keys and Radio Technology in Smart Buildings
By Nick Wood, Insight SiP
The direction of travel seems clear enough: Digital keys are likely to replace physical ones entirely over time.
How Much Impact Will AI Have on IoT Software Engineering?
By Steve Bennett, Wireless Logic
In theory, AI is a surefire way to raise productivity in software engineering, but the reality may not be quite so cut-and-dried.
LEDs Push Wireless Power Further
By Rebecca Pool
An LED alternative to laser wireless power transfer from the Institute of Science Tokyo uses adaptive optics and AI beam steering to charge indoor IoT devices 5 meters away.
Smarter Cameras Need More Than Edge AI to Protect Privacy
By Pat Brans
Axis Communications and Pimloc show how masking, encryption, anonymization, and
governance can protect privacy without destroying useful evidence.
The Security AI That Learns the Language of Movement
By Pat Brans
UNC Charlotte researchers use edge AI to learn normal motion, predict what comes next, and flag anomalies for human review.
India Hardens Its Cyber Defenses
By Rebecca Pool
As cyberthreats target critical infrastructure and India’s online population tops 1 billion, digital resilience is now a national security priority.

articles.title: Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor
articles.text:
A mixture of expert agentic AI systems can focus on their tasks with or without a commanding general, but challenges remain in drawing boundaries between human and AI effort.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss recent developments and challenges when using agentic AI for chip design, with Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at Cadence; Harrison Balistreri, head of business development and strategic partnerships at ChipAgents; Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA; and Anand Thiruvengadam, executive director and head of AI product management at Synopsys. This roundtable was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is the third part of a three-part series. Part one is here. Part two is here.
L-R: Synopsys’ Thiruvengadam; Keysight’s Petr; Cadence’s Graham; ChipAgents’ Balistreri; and Siemens’ Balasubramanian.
SE: Many agentic flows involve a mixture of experts (MoE) or a hierarchy of multi-agents with some type of leader at the top. What developments are you seeing there? Is it a top-down, military-style organization with various security and access clearances, or more of a horizontal team?
Graham: It is becoming much flatter than an army. If you’d asked me a year ago, I might have said, yes, it is a big hierarchy of agents. There will be mini agents, sub agents, and low agents. There will be generals and lieutenants and whatever else, all the way up. But AI in general, not just EDA, we are migrating much more toward a flat set of skills, or capabilities, or features, or knowledge, or whatever the word is you want to use to describe it. Everything is overloaded with terms. What we’re seeing becomes a much more dynamic, task-based organization of skills into almost dynamic agents. There is one general, if you like, or commander.
Balasubramanian: Orchestrator.
Graham: Right. And everything else below tends to be much flatter. I can pick and choose quickly to assemble my troops, but it’s much less like an army with a mechanized division and an airborne division, or something else. We have troops. Those troops have skills, and we assemble the right troops for the task dynamically, because we’re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality.
Petr: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments. They can play individually, or they can play together. They can also play synchronously or asynchronously to achieve certain tunes and then play together.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. Even if it’s flat, the key thing is that everyone knows their part, and they also know how they connect to everyone else. Everyone knows the end goal. Nothing is siloed. They all play by the same tune. If you look at a symphony orchestra, everyone knows everyone else. They can read the notes. They know what to do, what not to do, how to do it.
Petr: There are borders, guardrails. They all ground it.
Balasubramanian: The term I see quite a bit is headless agents. There’s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it’s been quite popular on the software side. It’s coming here, and what I see going forward is customers are interacting with tools. They won’t even know what the tool is. From our side, we are going to build agentic capabilities coming out of the physical engines, or deterministic engines around those engines, and that’s going to be an agent on its own. It can talk to other agents. It can understand different formats and where it sits. It can talk to understand design. Designers can interact with it, make it do work. That’s where the future is going.
Thiruvengadam: What Matt said is very interesting. We are essentially making the point that you should be thinking about digital organization—human organization, human hierarchy, digital hierarchy, roughly speaking —which is correct. But also, the fluidity of that is very important. It won’t be a rigid, hard structure. Ebb and flow will happen. It can change, depending on the complexity of the commands. The fluidity is very important. You will have a layer that orchestrates and calls upon ‘resources’ as needed to execute. This is very important. At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it’s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again. We are talking about taking layer after layer of abstraction away, one by one, but we’re not there yet.
Balistreri: We have products where agents propose hypotheses and do tournament-style ranking. We have a judging agent, but there’s a lot of nuance in this idea of agents, where you could throw many agents at the problem. But if they all come up with similar hypotheses for the problem, it doesn’t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is. It has a lot to do with how you manage context, and it comes back to local versus global context. It doesn’t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context. To get the benefit of deploying agents at scale, you need to manage which hypotheses each agent generates and where that context comes from. To do that, you also can’t have point agents. You can’t do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow. The full flow requires encoding in your agent loops how to view some of this context and how to manage that, so that you get the benefit of many parallel agents instead of them just trying to converge on the same thing.
Graham: There are two sides to that, and I agree for the most part. But I’ll draw a parallel to how synthesis changed electronic design. The vast majority of gates built now are synthesized gates. The agent writes RTL. Then, RTL gets synthesized. But there is still a certain percentage, depending on the application, that must be either hand-synthesized or laid out by hand. There will still be significant opportunity to accelerate the tools. I wouldn’t call it a point agent necessarily. But in agentifying the tool for a specific task, a smaller percentage will still need to be hand-coded, in the same way that we still hand-assemble some instructions for a PC or for any compute platform. Expecting 100% autonomy is setting too high a bar that I don’t know we can achieve. I don’t think it’s realistic or even worthwhile. Setting it at 99-point-some-odd-nines still leaves a huge amount of work to be done, and accelerating the tools themselves is still important, but I agree that it’s not the bulk of the time.
Balistreri: This might be an unpopular opinion in this room, but we can talk about accelerating existing tools, or we can talk about new tools entirely. When we talk to our customers, one of the biggest bottlenecks in taping out their chips is that they don’t have enough on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools. Can you rearchitect tools to be optimized for agent use, speed up runtime, and run more tools in parallel? Then there’s the other question of, ‘Do the models subsume it?’ In some of the complex tasks that are still hand-placed, there is an opportunity for models to take that on and solve extremely complex problems that humans just couldn’t hold in their heads. Think about all those tables you had to look at on the wall. Back in the day, you were laying sheets across a giant table to look at the resistance and capacitance and placing them for analog. All of that, I think, can be captured inside of models.
Graham: It can be. The question is, how soon will it be efficient? We’ve spent a huge amount of time solving that problem deterministically, algorithmically, and mathematically so that we get the right answer every single time. What you’re proposing is, ‘Can we use a probabilistic model to solve those problems more efficiently?’ Today, ‘no’ is the very clear answer. With the speed of technological advancement, will that be compute-efficient and dollar-efficient in the next 2 years, 8 years, 10 years?
Thiruvengadam: I agree. The key point, again, is the march of nines. The march of nines will kick in, and you’ve got a 99.99999. You need to get 100% accuracy. We’re talking about subsuming two EDA tools into models.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. In chip design, being 99.99% accurate is a failure. All it takes is one picosecond and you have a whole violation.
Petr: We keep forgetting that we still have not fully understood all the physics. Every single model we have is a simplification of the real world. It’s an error of an error of an error of an error. No matter how well you go on the whole agentic framework, at some point, there’s a trade-off somewhere. And if you don’t capture that, your chip is dead. We spent decades optimizing the simulator engines to get deterministic results. There’s always an argument in those AI frameworks, ‘Oh, just run reinforcement learning. It can do it.’ Fair, it can. But my mathematically based optimizer is still faster and more accurate. Why would I want to do that?
Thiruvengadam: It’s important to understand that the march of nines is a problem in software. Why would it not be a problem in hardware? In chip design, it’s even more of a problem. In software, they talk about getting 100%. Failure is an important part. In hardware, costs are so high that the march of nines becomes an even bigger problem.
Balasubramanian: As we go down the flow, the band of how much error you can tolerate drops drastically.
SE: In an orchestral multi-agentic flow, who has a kill switch to prevent agents from burning through tokens and trying forever to gain 100% coverage closure, for example?
Graham: This is part of the prep before you deploy, which must be part of the infrastructure. We all have infrastructure this must sit on — the guardrails. There are still infinite problems in IC design and verification. Fundamentally, it’s an infinite or near-infinite problem, so there must be guardrails somewhere on how much time, how many tokens, and what the tool covers, etc. One thing EDA has been good at over the years is having tool providers address that with customers, having customers understand the best ROI trade-offs, and pushing us to provide them. Up until now, it was cycles on a given problem. We get the number of CPU cycles we think we need to do, whether we get them in the cloud or on-prem or whatever, for one of the thousand tasks you have to do from RTL to GDS. Now we’re adding tokens to those, but we need the same guardrails. We know this. Our customers employ entire departments of people to optimize this exact problem.
Petr: Infinite loops are not new to us. Every mathematical problem has infinite loops. If you get into those trenches, we have solutions.
SE: What about IP ownership if you’re using an agent for a design that you sell to a customer, or they use your agent for their design, who owns what IP?
Balasubramanian: IP ownership is one of the biggest concerns I’m hearing about, both from our side as the tool provider and from the customer side. Yes, [agents] can write code, but the challenge is that all it takes is one copyrighted piece of code getting into your codebase, and if you don’t verify it, you’re going to get a loss. That’s one thing. Second, the most important thing is, I always tell people that any prompt you do, that’s your IQ. You’re doing your foundation, you’re using Claude Code, and you’re letting your designers do certain things. Their prompt will be, ‘This is how I’m going to be solving this routing problem. Can you do this?’ Your prompt is pretty much your IP. You’re telling some people the algorithm for how to do certain things, and there is a lot of talk about, ‘They’re not going to look at it.’ But every prompt is necessary to the LLM providers. If it goes outside of the air gap, it’s a problem. So IP protection is going to be very key. How do you expose code outside, especially source code? That’s going to be very key, and that’s a big concern coming up.
Petr: Another problem is that U.S. copyright does not allow us to copyright code that has been generated by an AI. That means every chip designed by an AI isn’t copyrightable.
Balasubramanian: Yes, because LLMs are not [copyrightable].
Thiruvengadam: The key distinction is that we are not talking about a chip that’s 100% designed by AI with no human intervention.
Petr: There’s a clause in the copyright that says the majority of the [design] has to be done by a human and, I’m sorry to say that, but the majority is not going to be.
Balistreri: I want to recap a bit and then get to this point. There are many problems, many layers of problems, with deploying AI in a high ROI way that organizations will accept meets their security requirements. One is cost. We solve that at the harness layer. The same model, doing like-for-like tasks, uses 40% fewer tokens. Our own model is open-weight and performs similarly, but at lower cost. Then there’s the full-flow problem, which is where you need the ontology. You can’t just do point acceleration. Then there’s the autonomous problem, which is the trust. Are there going to be critical errors? Are those gated and built into your system so you can’t produce things? Then there’s the IP and security issue, and it’s a pretty simple question. Do you want to send your inference over the public internet to a model provider that is building chips that compete with your chips? If you use frontier models in your agentic layer, whatever agents you use, you run that risk. Some don’t even have zero data retention. The clear answer to us — in a highly security-focused industry, where your design and design flow itself is IP — is that you need a solution with a custom model you can deploy on-prem. That also solves the IP question. I’m not a copyright lawyer, but if the design never leaves your environment, it’s de facto still yours. It’s not copyrighted per se, but no one else can access it.
Petr: Don’t underestimate reverse engineering.

articles.title: AgInvest 2026 in Coimbatore puts farm economics at the centre of AgriTech investment
articles.text:
AgInvest 2026 in Coimbatore puts farm economics at the centre of AgriTech investment
AgInvest 2026 will bring founders, investors and research institutions to Coimbatore to back revenue-stage AgriTech startups focused on measurable economic value, field validation and scalable business models.
Coimbatore-based FounderPassion Foundation will host AgInvest 2026, an investment summit for revenue stage agriculture startups, on 26 September 2026. The event will bring AgriTech founders, investors, research institutions and agricultural bodies onto one platform at a time when AgriTech investment in India has become cautious and selective. Its message to founders is direct: build technology that solves agriculture's biggest economic problems, rather than adding to the long list of farm apps.
A sector working through a funding reset
FounderPassion Foundation is a not-for-profit Section 8 Startup Accelerator set up in 2018. It works with agriculture and sustainability startups, with a particular focus on ventures from Tier 2 and 3 cities that can influence the rural economy.
The summit arrives as Indian AgriTech works through a prolonged slowdown. According to Tracxn data, AgriTech companies in India raised $134 million in equity funding across 41 rounds up to July 2026, down from $198 million across 77 rounds in the same period of 2025. Annual funding in the sector had peaked at about $1.19 billion in 2021. Capital has not disappeared, but it has become far more selective about which models it backs.
What AgInvest 2026 will cover
The summit looks well beyond farm-management software. Focus areas identified by the organisers include food supply chains, preservation and storage, post-harvest technology, farm-to-market systems, precision and predictive agriculture, water technology, soil health, Agri-FinTech, agri-biotech, animal husbandry, sustainable feed, residue management and agro forestry. Technologies such as IoT, AI, drones, robotics and decision-support systems cut across these categories.
According to the organisers, invitations have gone out to investors including Indian Angel Network, IvyCap Ventures, Ankur Capital, TIH IITB, Chennai Angels, Mudhal Partners and some more VC’s. Institutional invitees include a-IDEA at ICAR-NAARM, Pusa Krishi at ICAR-IARI, the Technology Innovation Hub at IIT Bombay, Agrinnovate India and NABI.
Why AgriTech investment is moving from scale to value
The organisers frame the event around a clear change in investor priorities. Instead of rewarding the number of farmers reached, investors are now asking who the paying customer is, what measurable problem is being solved, how often that problem occurs, what return the buyer gets from adopting the technology, and whether the business can turn profitable without repeated rounds of external capital. Recent industry commentary points the same way, with investors describing the slowdown as a structural reset linked to a global shift towards profitability, rather than a retreat from the sector.
For founders, the organisers argue that the market is wider than farmers alone. Some of the most scalable businesses may sell to banks, insurers, farmer producer organisations (FPOs), processors, exporters and equipment operators, opening up B2B and B2B2F models. Extraction for the pharma, nutrition and wellness industries is flagged as another high-potential segment.
More than a one-day event
Led by Founder and Managing Director Vijayakumar NRR, FounderPassion Foundation is positioning AgInvest 2026 as the start of a longer engagement between startups, investors and institutions rather than a standalone pitch day. The organisers plan to work with incubators and accelerators to support startups from problem identification and prototyping through field validation, commercial pilots and investment.
This matters because AgriTech startups need more than capital and conventional mentoring. They need access to real farms, FPOs, laboratories, research institutions, machinery and early customers, and building those links takes time.
How does a field-to-market pathway help AgriTech startups raise capital
Unlike an app, an agricultural product has to prove itself across seasons, crops and regions before a buyer commits. A field-to-market pathway moves a startup through defined stages: research, prototype, field trial, farmer validation, commercial pilot and scale, with investment following the evidence gathered at each step.
For investors, this means startups arrive with field data rather than projections. The organisers suggest tracking outcomes such as farmer income, productivity per hectare, input savings, water efficiency, reduction in post-harvest losses, customer retention and capital efficiency. These metrics link a startup's performance directly to economic value on the ground.
What to watch after 26 September
The organisers see AgriTech less as a narrow sector and more as a meeting point for AI, climate technology, FinTech, deeptech and manufacturing. Dedicated capital remains thin, though. A recent industry report noted that of more than 210 venture, private equity and government-backed funds launched in India since 2024, only 23 specifically target AgriTech. If AgInvest 2026 can move a cohort of startups from field trials to paid pilots with investors tracking the data, it could offer a working template for how regional incubators channel capital into agriculture's harder, infrastructure-heavy problems. The real measure will be how many conversations in Coimbatore turn into pilots and term sheets in the months that follow.

articles.title: Airbus turned the Steam Deck into a controller for a prototype Mars rover — Valve handheld PC gives engineers command of the ExoMars platform during testing
articles.text:
Airbus turned the Steam Deck into a controller for a prototype Mars rover — Valve handheld PC gives engineers command of the ExoMars platform during testing
Engineers have turned Valve's handheld PC into the fanciest remote control ever
Valve's Steam Deck portable PC, the same one you might play your favorite games on, isn't just for fun, as Airbus has just proven. The aerospace firm is using the Deck to control a prototype Mars rover throughout its development and testing process.
The ExoMars rover, a device that will be autonomous when it reaches the Red Planet, is being developed in the UK by Airbus. The rover and its Steam Deck companion made an appearance in a video shared by YouTube personality Tom Scott following a visit to Airbus' facility. And while ExoMars is being tested on Earth, it's hoped that it will eventually be capable of controlling itself when it rolls out onto the Martian terrain.
For now, engineers need a way to control the rover during its development and testing in a Mars-like environment. And for that, Airbus has settled on a Steam Deck.
The video shows a Steam Deck running unspecified custom software. Just like playing the games Steam Deck owners are familiar with, Scott can be seen using the thumbsticks, triggers, and face buttons as a method for controlling the rover.
While novel, the decision to use a Steam Deck in this way probably shouldn't be all that surprising. It's a handheld PC in every sense of the word — it's powered by Linux and has both physical and touchscreen controls, not to mention Wi-Fi and Bluetooth support. If you're so inclined, you can even install Windows on a Steam Deck, too.
All of these things make the Steam Deck the perfect way to control something as advanced as a Mars rover. Doubly so if specialist software is required, something that traditional controllers like Sony's DualSense and Microsoft's Xbox controllers can't offer. With that in mind, it's perhaps only a matter of time until we see Valve's Steam Frame also used for testing of a future Mars rover.
As for today, Airbus teams in Stevenage, UK, are working on a project to design the mechanical, thermal, and propulsion systems for the landing platform that will help a rover land on Mars in 2030. That rover will be officially called the Rosalind Franklin, and getting it to Mars safely will be "the culmination of more than 20 years’ work," says Kata Escott, the managing director of Airbus Defence and Space UK. Even if Valve's handheld doesn't prove necessary for controlling the Franklin rover once it's on Mars, it can still claim a cool spot in the history of the platform's development.

Oliver Haslam has written about technology of all shapes and sizes for over 15 years, both online and in print. He's fascinated by how personal computing continues to change as tower PCs give way to foldable phones and beyond.

articles.title: How the US handed China control of the rare earth supply chain
articles.text:
MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.
Credit:
David McNew/Getty Images
All of these devices function because of 17 metals collectively known as rare earth elements. The scientists who gave the group that name in 1794 created a misnomer. Cerium alone is about as common in the Earth’s crust as copper.
However, separating rare earth minerals from one another and from raw ore is intensely difficult. As a result, countries that control the processing of rare earth minerals have a lot of political leverage.
China processes most of the rare earth minerals used around the world, and it isn’t just consumer electronics that depend on Chinese exports. The US military’s F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines need rare earths too.
I spent years adjudicating war games for the US Navy. War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint.
China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a series of export controls issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend—at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very big stick.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
The US has rare earth minerals, but few mines. For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing. MP Materials’ Mountain Pass mine and processing facility restarted in California in 2017.
Credit:
Tmy350/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA
China, which mined about 60 percent of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about 91 percent of separation and refining.
Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising.
Why rebuilding is slow
The US Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation, and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years. Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons.
China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the US has far fewer experts. Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023.
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this US Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.
Credit:
USGS
The US government has committed more than $7 billion since April 2025 to try to rebuild US rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought $400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials in 2025, giving it 15 percent ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028.
The Commerce Department also signed a letter of intent in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma.
But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult.
What happens on November 10
On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced six wide-ranging export control measures. One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up 0.1 percent or more of its value, or if it used Chinese rare earth technology.
Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses.
What stays in place
Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the heavier rare earths.
Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets—critical to speakers and electrical motors—because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “day to day” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production only with Beijing’s approval.
On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put 10 US companies on its export control list. Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems, and military vehicles. Two of them—MP Materials and USA Rare Earth—are the federally backed American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain.
Beijing said its move was a response to a similar move by the Pentagon. My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing.
An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice.
Rebuilding a US rare earths supply chain would remove most US dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars, and separation produces acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues.
Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the US being cut off unilaterally. Japan has run this play with some success, but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad.
President Xi’s Sept. 24, 2026, meeting with Trump may help determine the status of the Nov. 10 restrictions, but the larger conflict over leverage will continue.

articles.title: BHIM MyUPI brings 9 UPI services into one AI assistant
articles.text:
BHIM MyUPI brings 9 UPI services into one AI assistant
BHIM MyUPI lets users track transactions, manage Autopay mandates, raise complaints and check fraud risks through a conversational assistant inside the BHIM app.
UPI support is getting a chat window. BHIM MyUPI, launched by NPCI BHIM Services Limited, brings nine UPI-related services into an AI-powered assistant within the BHIM Payments App.
Launched at Global Fintech Fest 2026, MyUPI offers 24/7 assistance in everyday language, allowing users to check transactions, raise complaints, manage mandates and access safety tools without moving between multiple screens or support channels.
The feature currently supports English, Hindi, Telugu, Tamil and Bengali, with more regional languages planned.
MyUPI puts UPI support in one place
MyUPI lets users view UPI transactions across their linked bank accounts and UPI apps in one place. They can select a transaction and seek help directly within the BHIM app.
The assistant also handles eligible payment complaints. Users can raise an issue, receive a complaint reference number and track its status without leaving the app.
Another feature, Transaction Replay, lets users re-initiate eligible earlier UPI payments, including P2P and P2M transactions originally made through another UPI app. Any new payment still requires authentication through the UPI PIN.
Recurring payments get a similar treatment. MyUPI provides a consolidated view of UPI Autopay mandates across linked accounts and apps. Users can view mandate details and, where permitted, pause, resume or cancel them.
Users can also de-link their mobile-linked UPI Number if they no longer want to receive payments through it, while continuing to receive money through their UPI ID where applicable.
A safety check before the money moves
MyUPI brings security tools into the same conversational interface.
Its Pay Safe feature allows users to enter a UPI ID or upload a QR code to verify the payee name before making a payment. The idea is simple: check who is receiving the money before sending it.
There is also a Safety Switch for situations such as a lost phone, suspected account compromise, unexpected debit or suspicious message. Users can use it to block a linked bank account and prevent further transactions from that account.
The assistant can also answer questions about suspected scam messages and commonly reported UPI fraud methods.
Payment actions continue to require authentication through the user's UPI PIN, so the conversational interface does not replace the existing payment authorisation process.
Making UPI support more conversational
The multilingual approach could matter as digital payments spread beyond India's major cities. For users who find conventional app menus difficult to navigate, asking a question in a familiar language could offer a simpler way to find the right support option.
MyUPI is available through the Quick Actions section of the BHIM Payments App, bringing transaction information, complaints, mandates and safety controls into a single interface.
Lalitha Nataraj, Managing Director and CEO of NPCI BHIM Services Limited, said MyUPI is intended to add a “proactive trust layer” to BHIM, helping users seek information, resolve concerns and take action with greater clarity.
For BHIM, the bigger test now is whether that conversational layer can make UPI easier to understand when a payment fails, a mandate needs attention, or something looks suspicious.

articles.title: Microsoft: September Windows updates break Always On VPN connections
articles.text:
Microsoft has notified IT administrators that users may experience Always On VPN connection issues after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates.
Always On VPN is a remote access solution that replaces the legacy DirectAccess technology and works with domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices.
It is available on Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server, and it runs seamlessly in the background, establishing a secure tunnel back to the corporate network automatically whenever a device connects to the internet.
Always On VPN also lets administrators define which apps and services can use the VPN connection, and it supports modern VPN protocols like IKEv2 and SSTP, plus multi-factor authentication (MFA) for better security.
In a service alert seen by BleepingComputer and shared by Microsoft MVP Susan Bradley, Microsoft says that affected customers may experience issues when their systems attempt to connect to their organization's enterprise network via Always On VPN.
"This issue can occur when the VPN is configured to automatically try another connection method if the initial connection fails (for example, when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP)," Microsoft said.
"Affected VPN connections might remain in a 'Connecting' state or repeatedly attempt to connect without succeeding. Subsequent connection attempts might also display the error: 'The specified port is already in use.'"
| Affected Versions | Originating update | 
|---|---|
| Windows 11, version 26H1 | KB5124012 | 
| Windows 11, version 25H2 | KB5124008 | 
| Windows 11, version 24H2 | KB5124008 | 
While Microsoft is still working on a permanent solution, it shared a temporary fix for affected customers that requires them to choose one of the two VPN tunneling protocols to work around the issue.
"IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," it said.
"Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements."
This month's cumulative updates have been linked to multiple other issues affecting both home and enterprise Windows users.
One week ago, Microsoft released emergency updates to fix Hyper-V issues, Remote Desktop Services failures, and USB audio problems also triggered by the September 2026 updates.
It also shared a temporary workaround for a separate issue that blocks some Windows 11 users from logging in with valid domain credentials and announced that it is working to address another bug that may cause the built-in File History backup feature in Windows to stop working.

articles.title: Aides carburant 2026 : l'État étend la portée de plusieurs dispositifs, voilà ce qu'il y a à savoir
articles.text:
Le gouvernement vient de faire une série d'annonces pour soutenir les Français en cette période de crise énergétique. Les dispositifs d'aides au carburant vont ainsi être renforcés.
Le prix à la pompe en ce moment fait mal aux Français, à tel point que, selon le ministre des Comptes publics David Amiel, la consommation de carburant s'est effondrée de 30% entre le 11 et le 20 septembre derniers. Devant une situation critique, le gouvernement était obligé de réagir, ce qu'il vient de faire avec la publication d'un communiqué de presse annonçant l'extension de plusieurs dispositifs.
L'aide grand rouleurs concernera dorénavant près de 5,5 millions de Français
450 millions d'euros. C'est ce que va coûter l'extension des dispositifs d'aides aux carburant décidée par le gouvernement. Et la première qui va être soutenue, c'est l'aide dite pour les « grands rouleurs ».
D'un montant de 100 euros pour les trois prochains mois, le public qui pourra la solliciter est agrandi. Alors que jusque-là, il fallait un revenu fiscal de référence égal ou inférieur à 16 880 euros par part, elle pourra à partir du 1er octobre concerner les « Français gagnant jusqu'à 2 050€ pour une personne seule, 4 070€ net pour un couple ou 6 100€ pour un couple avec deux enfants ». La population éligible passe ainsi de 3 millions à près de 5,5 millions de personnes.
Le montant maximum de prime carburant exonérées d'impôts passe à 1000 euros
Pour ce qui est de la prime carburant employeur, la prime que peut donner l'employeur pour financer les frais de carburant ou d'alimentation du véhicule d'un employé, les conditions sont elles aussi améliorées.
S'il n'y a pas de montant maximal à cette prime, initialement, seuls 300 euros pouvaient être exonérés de cotisations sociales et d'impôts. Un montant qui a ensuite été augmenté pour passer à 600 euros, puis, avec les annonces faites hier par le gouvernement, désormais à 1000 euros. Enfin, le chèque énergie ne subit lui pas de changement durant cette période.

articles.title: Steven Spielberg et Chris Columbus vont bien faire Gremlins 3... mais il y a un problème
articles.text:
Warner Bros. a annoncé ce mercredi 23 septembre le report de Gremlins 3. Prévu pour le 19 novembre 2027, le film sortira finalement dans les salles américaines le 6 octobre 2028, près d’un an plus tard, pour la période d’Halloween. Warner n’a pas expliqué ce choix, mais Deadline rappelle que le premier week-end d’octobre a déjà réussi au studio avec Joker, sorti le 4 octobre 2019 aux États-Unis, qui avait rapporté 1,078 milliard de dollars dans le monde. David Zaslav, CEO de Warner Bros. Discovery, avait officialisé le projet en novembre 2025, lors d’une conférence avec les investisseurs. Les Gremlins reviendront au cinéma 38 ans après Gremlins 2 : La Nouvelle Génération, sorti en 1990.
Warner Bros. a accompagné l’annonce d’un premier teaser de 11 secondes, publié sur ses réseaux sociaux. On y aperçoit brièvement un mogwai avant l’affichage de la nouvelle date, avec la mention « Only In Theaters » (« uniquement au cinéma »). Le film ne sortira qu’en salles, sans passage simultané en streaming, à l’ancienne, et c’est tant mieux.
Un monument de la pop culture des années 1980
Le studio n’a encore dévoilé ni le titre officiel, ni le casting, ni l’intrigue de Gremlins 3. L’équipe, elle, est connue : Chris Columbus, scénariste du premier volet et réalisateur des deux premiers Harry Potter, assurera la réalisation et la production. Il retrouve pour l’occasion Steven Spielberg, de retour au poste de producteur exécutif aux côtés d’Eleanor Columbus, de la société de production Maiden Voyage. Le scénario est quant à lui confié à Hannah Marks, qui s’appuie sur un premier jet de Chris Columbus et du duo Zach Lipovsky et Adam Stein, réalisateurs de Destination finale : Bloodlines.
Sorti en 1984 sous la direction de Joe Dante, le film original Gremlins est devenu un classique du cinéma fantastique. Ses scènes violentes ont poussé, avec celles d’Indiana Jones et le Temple maudit, à la création de la classification PG-13 aux États-Unis, qui signale un film déconseillé aux moins de 13 ans. L’histoire suit le jeune Billy Peltzer, qui se voit offrir Gizmo, un mogwai aussi mystérieux qu’adorable. Une adoption soumise à des consignes strictes : ne jamais l’exposer à la lumière vive, ne jamais le mouiller et, surtout, ne jamais le nourrir après minuit. Les règles sont vite enfreintes. Mouillé par accident, Gizmo donne naissance à d’autres mogwais, bien moins sages. Nourris après minuit, ils se changent en gremlins et sèment un chaos sanglant et drôle dans une petite ville américaine, en pleine période des fêtes.
Produit pour un budget modeste de 11 millions de dollars, le premier film avait engrangé plus de 212 millions de dollars au box-office mondial, dont 153 millions en Amérique du Nord. Sa suite de 1990, Gremlins 2 : La Nouvelle Génération, avait fait nettement moins bien : 41,5 millions de dollars de recettes en Amérique du Nord, pour un budget estimé entre 30 et 50 millions de dollars. Sa satire des grandes entreprises, avec des gremlins lâchés dans un gratte-ciel de bureaux, lui a depuis valu un statut de film culte.
Un passage de témoin entre générations
Warner Bros. distribue les films Gremlins depuis 1984. Lors de l’annonce du film, Jesse Ehrman, président du développement et de la production chez Warner Bros. Pictures, se disait « plus qu’impatient » de ramener Gremlins « pour les fans de toujours comme pour une toute nouvelle génération ».
Le film est coproduit par Amblin Entertainment, la société de Steven Spielberg, et par 26th Street Pictures, celle de Chris Columbus.
