articles.title: Stockholm’s Spiich raises €3 million to let AI handle admin work while sales teams focus on customers | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Spiich, a Stockholm-based AI sales agent startup, has raised a €3 million Seed round. This announcement comes ten months after the company raised a €600k pre-Seed round, bringing its total funding to €3.6 million.
The funding round was led by Ugly Duckling Ventures, a Copenhagen-based venture firm backing Nordic B2B software and technology companies. The round also saw participation from new investors Alliance VC and Cherry Ventures, while pre-Seed backer Ampli Ventures returned with a follow-on investment. Its backers also include angel investors from Lovable, Neo4j, Tandem Health and OpenAI.
Louise Lachmann, General Partner, Ugly Duckling Ventures, said, “Every sales tool of the last decade promised to give reps their time back, and most of them delivered another system to keep updated. Spiich is the first we’ve seen that does the non-selling work rather than assisting with it.
“What convinced us wasn’t the demo, it was what happened after go-live: accounts expanding within weeks because teams kept finding more work to hand over. Johan and Dennis pair engineering judgement well above their stage with a commercial instinct you rarely find in the same founding team. That’s why we led the round.
Founded in Stockholm in June 2025 by Johan Torssell and Dennis Hadzialic, Spiich builds AI agents that take on the prospecting, meeting prep, CRM updates and follow-up work that usually keeps reps away from customers, work that Salesforce estimates eats up 78% of a salesperson’s time. Rather than a wave of AI sales startups trying to automate the salesperson, Spiich is making a contrarian bet.
The company says selling is fundamentally human and sees building AI agents capable of absorbing everything around the sale, leading to relationship-building that actually closes deals. Its thesis is working, with Spiich now serving more than 50 customers across 15 countries in Europe, the US and South America, including NORNORM, ProfitMetrics, Zaver, Airmee, Rebaba and Epiminds.
Its customers have reportedly doubled their customer meetings, cut prospecting time by 90% and tripled their market coverage. The company reports 100%+ month-on-month ARR growth in the first half of 2026, 160%+ net revenue retention, and more than 50,000 deals closed by customers through its platform.
“Have you ever bought anything from an AI agent? Almost nobody has. You buy from someone you trust to deliver. Every deal I have ever closed came down to that. We didn’t build Spiich to replace salespeople. We built it so they can finally sell,” said Torssell, co-founder and CEO of Spiich.
Spiich will use the new funding to grow its engineering and go-to-market teams as it targets expansion across Europe. Like every other AI startup, Spiich is also positioning itself as more than a productivity tool. Since it spans every meeting, email, internal note, and external signal tied to a customer relationship, Spiich aims to become a “system of intelligence and action” for the sales team.

articles.title: How SWE-Serve Exposes the Gap Between Local Tests and Live Serving | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
An AI coding agent’s patch can pass tests yet fail when the server loads a real model and handles requests. Evaluating changes to inference-serving software therefore requires checking the full serving path, including whether the system returns correct results through its public interface.
Developed with input from the SGLang team, SWE-Serve evaluates this gap with 53 tasks derived from merged changes to SGLang, an open-source system for serving large language models. Across 19 tasks with live-serving checks, the same patches passed 69.4% of the time when those checks were excluded, but only 45.9% with the complete verifier. About one in three patches that passed the other checks failed live-serving tests.
Quick links: Read the paper | Explore the leaderboard | Run SWE-Serve on GitHub
What SWE-Serve tests
Existing repository-level benchmarks evaluate coding agents across general software-engineering tasks, while inference benchmarks often concentrate on kernel generation or performance optimization. SWE-Serve instead tests repository-scale changes across the inference-serving stack, including model enablement, decoding, caching, scheduling, serving APIs, and runtime performance.
To evaluate this broader engineering work, SWE-Serve turns 83 merged SGLang pull requests into 53 executable tasks across six inference-engineering families.
| Engineering family | Tasks | 
|---|---|
| Speculative and advanced decoding | 14 | 
| Model and backend enablement | 12 | 
| Kernels, quantization, and performance | 8 | 
| Serving APIs and runtime correctness | 8 | 
| Caching and runtime state | 7 | 
| Distributed execution and scheduling | 4 | 
Twelve tasks run on CPU, while 41 use a single NVIDIA H100. This first release doesn’t evaluate other inference engines, multi-GPU execution, or multi-node serving.
Thirty-seven tasks come from a single upstream pull request. The other 16 combine two to six related changes. In total, the benchmark draws on 83 merged SGLang pull requests. The SGLang team, a launch partner for SWE-Serve, contributed ideas for identifying challenging tasks, suggested particularly demanding pull requests, and helped shape our approach to verifying correctness.
Each task gives the agent an instruction and a containerized SGLang checkout from before the target change. The agent’s patch passes if it satisfies the task’s hidden verifier on the declared hardware. It is never compared with the reference implementation.
These are substantial changes. The median reference solution modifies 553 lines across seven files. A typical verifier has seven tests for the new behavior and 10 regression tests. Nineteen tasks start a real server, and three enforce a calibrated performance gate on an H100.
What one task looks like
One task asks the agent to add serving support for dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) Qwen3.5 models. Starting from a revision without Qwen3.5 support, the agent must make both the 0.8B dense model and the 35B-A3B MoE model load and serve through the normal SGLang interfaces on one H100.
Its verifier checks model registration, configuration and weight loading, image and video inputs, OpenAI-compatible requests, native batched generation, log probabilities, and execution through the MoE model’s routed experts.
What live serving tests catch
Some failures only appear once a real server starts. The SGLang team contributed ideas for end-to-end verification, including recommendations for specific model-serving tests. SWE-Serve includes 19 tasks that load the required model and test the agent’s patch through a live serving interface.
Across these tasks, the same 627 patches pass 45.9% of the time under the complete verifier. When the live serving tests are excluded, that rate rises to 69.4%. In other words, 147 patches changed from fail to pass when the live serving tests were excluded.
The 19 tasks contain 276 live serving tests. Of those, 242 are sourced or adapted from SGLang. The remaining 34 cover behavior introduced by the corresponding merged changes when no suitable upstream test was available.
The Gemma 4 MoE task makes the result concrete. Sixteen of 33 patches passed every other check but failed at least one live serving test. Those tests cover model loading, expert routing, text and image serving, and batched generation with correct ordering and log probabilities.
A SWE-Serve pass has a narrow meaning: the patch satisfies the benchmark verifier. SWE-Serve’s tests are not SGLang’s upstream review process. They don’t establish that an agent patch or benchmark reference solution is deployable, ready to merge, or endorsed by SGLang maintainers.
Where agents score lower
We divided the request-to-output path into four runtime domains: request handling and I/O, scheduling and request lifecycle, model execution, and KV-cache and runtime-resource management.
Across the best setting for each of the 11 models, the 26 tasks confined to one runtime domain have a 69.0% pass rate. The 27 tasks spanning more than one runtime domain have a 47.7% pass rate, a difference of 21.3 percentage points. Every model setting shows the same direction of difference.
Performance varies widely across models
Model performance varies substantially. Across each model’s best tested configuration, mean pass@1 ranges from 34.6% to 75.5%. No model scores highest in every task category, and configurations with similar overall scores can have very different costs and runtimes.
We evaluated 11 models and 31 model-effort configurations with mini-swe-agent, a minimal software-engineering agent that uses only Bash, under closed-book conditions. We tested the two Claude and three GPT-5.6 models at five effort levels; the other six models ran at one setting each.
Each configuration ran the complete 53-task benchmark three times. Each agent session was capped at 210 minutes and 350 steps. A task counts as solved only when the agent’s patch passes the complete verifier on the task’s declared hardware. The table reports the highest-scoring effort setting for each model.
| Model | Reasoning setting | pass@1(mean ± SD, 3 runs) | Mean cost/task | Mean wall time | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5 | max | 75% ± 3% | $17.40 | 57.5 min | 
| GPT-5.6 Sol | max | 75% ± 6% | $12.26 | 29.5 min | 
| Claude Sonnet 5 | xhigh | 64% ± 3% | $6.61 | 40.6 min | 
| Kimi K3 | max | 64% ± 5% | $7.24 | 99.9 min | 
| GPT-5.6 Luna | max | 64% ± 4% | $0.95 | 28.9 min | 
| GPT-5.6 Terra | max | 64% ± 4% | $5.06 | 25.5 min | 
| DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731) | max | 55% ± 4% | $0.69 | 36.4 min | 
| GLM-5.2 | max | 48% ± 2% | $2.10 | 34.0 min | 
| Gemini 3.6 Flash | high | 48% ± 6% | $4.84 | 37.3 min | 
| Laguna S 2.1 | max | 46% ± 5% | $0.33 | 56.9 min | 
| Inkling S | xhigh | 35% ± 3% | $0.44 | 17.6 min | 
Native harnesses didn’t improve the two leaders: GPT-5.6 Sol scored 73.6% in Codex and Claude Opus 5 scored 69.8% in Claude Code, versus 75.5% each with mini-swe-agent.
Cost doesn’t map cleanly to performance. Among the four models tied at 64%, mean cost ranges from $0.95 to $7.24 per task, while mean wall time ranges from 25.5 to 99.9 minutes.
No model leads all six engineering families, and models with the same overall score can have different strengths. The top score shows that many SWE-Serve tasks are within reach of current agents; the spread shows that performance is far from uniform.
How we validate the benchmark
We screened 786 potential task sources, built 156 executable candidates, and admitted 53.
Every admitted task was tested on its declared hardware. The unmodified repository had to fail the tests for the new behavior while continuing to pass regression tests. A reference patch had to pass the complete verifier. We also challenged the verifiers with agent-created patches, repairing, narrowing, or excluding tasks when we found a concrete problem.
Reported evaluations are closed-book. We block the public web and upstream source repositories, while allowing Hugging Face access for model weights, because an open-network pilot showed models retrieving task-specific upstream code. We audited all 1,749 trials behind the leaderboard; 196 prohibited retrieval attempts were blocked, and none succeeded. The paper describes the full qualification and evaluation-integrity process.
Run SWE-Serve
SWE-Serve includes the task environments, verifiers, and baseline configurations. It makes the gap between passing local checks and working through the full serving path measurable.
Explore the SWE-Serve leaderboard, then run SWE-Serve on GitHub to evaluate your coding agent on SGLang inference-engineering tasks.

articles.title: Megafiltración de 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' revela su nuevo final y más escenas inéditas que conectan con 'Doomsday'
articles.text:
El reestreno de Avengers: Endgame en Corea del Sur ha provocado la filtración de cuatro escenas adicionales que conectan el largometraje con Avengers: Doomsday, que llega a la cartelera en diciembre. El material extra de Avengers: Endgame Encore sirve como puente para el nuevo filme de los hermanos Russo y ya está causando reacciones bastante fuertes porque cambia el final de la aclamada cinta de 2019.
Las filmaciones no autorizadas desde el interior de las salas de cine coreanas no tardaron en llegar a plataformas como X (Twitter). A pesar de su rápida viralización, Marvel ha trabajado a destajo para eliminarlas a través de reclamos de derechos de autor, lo que habla de la legitimidad del material en cuestión.
Esto significa que muchos de los clips de Avengers: Endgame Encore ya no se encuentran disponibles en redes sociales. Aun así, han permanecido el tiempo suficiente para que el mundo tenga una idea más concreta sobre cómo los realizadores del largometraje pretenden conectarlo con Avengers: Doomsday.
El nuevo material de Avengers: Endgame se presenta mayormente como escenas postcréditos. Sin embargo, también hay un cambio crucial en la escena final de la película original que ya está generando cierta controversia, pero que los hermanos Russo seguramente creyeron indispensable para reintroducir al Steve Rogers/Capitán América de Chris Evans. Los detalles, a continuación.
Filtradas las escenas extra de Avengers: Endgame Encore que conectan con Doomsday
A partir de aquí, este artículo contiene SPOILERS tanto de la versión original de Avengers: Endgame, como del material adicional que se incorpora en la edición Encore que está llegando ahora a los cines. Si no quieres arruinarte alguna sorpresa, te recomendamos no continuar leyendo el artículo.
Las cuatro escenas extra de Avengers: Endgame Encore son estas:
- El nuevo final. La conclusión de Avengers: Endgame mostró a Steve Rogers y Peggy Carter cumpliendo con su tan postergado baile y compartiendo el resto de su vida. En el reestreno, ese momento se ve interrumpido cuando alguien golpea la puerta de la casa. El visitante es ni más ni menos que Loki en su variante de la TVA. Y cuando Peggy le pregunta si puede ayudarle con algo, este responde: "No, pero yo puedo ayudarles a los dos". Esto está despertando varias especulaciones respecto de cuándo se produce el encuentro, con muchos teorizando que puede ser antes de los eventos del final de la temporada 2 de Loki, la serie de Disney+. También hay mucho runrún sobre qué tipo de colaboración podría ofrecerles el hermano de Thor.
- La TVA y múltiples mundos incursionando. Un tema que promete ocupar espacio central en la trama de Avengers: Doomsday son las incursiones; es decir, la colisión entre diferentes mundos y universos. En Avengers: Endgame Encore se observa a Mobius y Ouroboros contemplando varias incursiones, con el multiverso comenzando a desmoronarse. El caso más notorio es el choque entre la aún desconocida Tierra-1127 y la Tierra-10005; este último, el mundo de los X-Men de FOX.
- Doom y Hulk. Otra de las escenas muestra a Bruce Banner siendo llevado a un búnker subterráneo tras los eventos de Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Allí, el científico graba un vídeo explicando que está trabajando en un nuevo suero para estabilizar a Hulk. También dice que nadie podrá entrar ni salir del sitio mientras esté abocado a sus tareas. Sin embargo, el Doctor Doom irrumpe en el refugio y le anuncia a Banner que ha llegado a "recogerle". Por ahora, no se sabe qué plan tiene Doom para con Hulk, pero la escena confirma que el personaje de Mark Ruffalo estará presente en Avengers: Doomsday, pese a que todavía no estaba anunciado.
- La máscara de Doom. En la última escena postcréditos de Avengers: Endgame Encore hay un claro guiño a Tony Stark. La misma muestra a Victor Von Doom forjando la máscara del Doctor Doom, de un modo muy similar a como Robert Downey Jr lo hizo como Stark en el primer filme de Iron Man. El sonido de los martillazos son idénticos, incluso. Esto ha disparado la teoría de que Von Doom podría presentarse como una variante de Tony Stark.
Sea como sea, la expectación de los fans está por el aire. Avengers: Endgame Encore llegará formalmente a los cines este viernes 25 de septiembre. Mientras que Avengers: Doomsday se estrenará el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: Elektroautos mit Falkenflügeltüren aus Saudi-Arabien
articles.text:
Ceer Exobot: Das sind die ersten Elektroautos aus Saudi-Arabien
Im November 2022 hatten der saudi-arabische Staatsfonds PIF und der Apple-Auftragsfertiger und E-Autobauer Foxconn das Unternehmen Ceer gegründet, um gemeinsam Elektroautos herzustellen. Mit einem Jahr Verspätung hat Ceer am 21. September 2026 seine ersten Serienmodelle vorgestellt.
Ceer Exobot: E-Limousine und E-Sedan
Dabei handelt es sich um eine Limousine (Sedan) und einen SUV, beide firmieren unter dem Namen Exobot, wie es in einer PIF-Mitteilung heißt. Ceer will die Elektroautos in einer eigens errichteten Fabrik am Roten Meer produzieren. Die Auslieferung der ersten Fahrzeuge, der sogenannten „First Edition“, ist für Frühjahr 2027 vorgesehen. Die Preise will Ceer „bald“ bekanntgeben.
Für Ende 2027 ist dann die Auslieferung der regulären Ausstattungslinie Exobot Plus geplant, wie das Handelsblatt schreibt. Weitere Modelle sollen folgen, darunter auch Elektroautos der Mittel- und Kompaktklasse. Bis 2031 will Ceer insgesamt sieben Modelle im Angebot haben.
BMW steuert Fahrzeugtechnik bei
Ob das Unternehmen die Fahrzeuge nach Deutschland bringt, ist nicht bekannt. Zuletzt war die Rede davon, dass Ceer zunächst vor allem im Nahen Osten und Afrika aktiv sein will. Dabei ist deutsche Hardware an Bord. Denn neben Rimac und Hyundai Transys ist BMW einer der Lieferanten von Fahrzeugtechnik für das saudi-arabische Unternehmen.
Die beiden jetzt angekündigten Modelle kommen jeweils mit drei E-Motoren, die alle vier Räder antreiben. Exobot Sedan und SUV bringen 850 Pferdestärken mit. Die Limousine soll in 2,6 Sekunden von null auf 100 Kilometer beschleunigen und eine Reichweite von 670 Kilometern haben. Beim SUV sind es 2,9 Sekunden und 560 Kilometer.
Elektroautos mit Schnellladefunktion
Beide verfügen über eine Schnellladefunktion, dank der der 112-Kilowattstunden-Akku in 30 Minuten von zehn auf 80 Prozent geladen werden kann. Im Inneren findet sich jeweils ein 48 Zoll breites 8K-Display. In Mittelkonsole und Fond hat Ceer weitere Bildschirme verbaut.
Auffälligstes Merkmal dürften aber die „Shahin Wing“ (Falkenflügel) genannten Türen sein. Diese sind direkt am Dach befestigt und öffnen nach oben. Zudem sollen die Elektroautos laut Handelsblatt speziell für den Einsatz in der Golfregion ausgelegt sein. So sollen eine besonders leistungsfähige Klimaanlage und eine wärmereflektierende Verglasung die Fahrer:innen vor dem heißen Klima schützen.

articles.title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
articles.text:
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.
Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
Audio-only Ray-Bans have arrived alongside more camera-equipped glasses. What’s missing? Privacy controls to address the ‘perv glasses’ backlash.
Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.
To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.
“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”
Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”
The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.
Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.
“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”
Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.
Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.
The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.
Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.
Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.
But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)
Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.
“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”
There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.
AI in your frames
All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.
“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”
The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.
Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.
Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.
“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.
Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)
That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.
More is more
Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.
So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

articles.title: IonQ Targets Quantum Error-Correction Bottleneck With Single-CPU Decoder
articles.text:
Quantum computing hardware and software company IonQ says it has developed a quantum error-correction decoder that runs in real time on a single conventional CPU, potentially reducing the classical computing overhead that can slow larger quantum systems. In simulations spanning up to 408 logical qubits, the company’s decoder added as little as 0.02% processing time under standard operating noise conditions.
Quantum computing gains its power through qubits, a special type of ‘bit’ that can have any of many states between the traditional binary on/off state of classical computing. The primary problem with qubits is that these ‘superimposed’ conditions that are neither on nor off are extremely fragile to environmental noise and very easily collapse, reverting to the binary state useless to quantum computing.
We call operational qubits ‘logical’ and the much larger number of additional qubits needed to find a collapsed ‘logical’ qubit as ‘physical’ qubits. The current solution is to have many more physical qubits able to locate each faulty (collapsed) logical qubit – but it requires slower classical computing to decode the information provided through the larger number physical qubits.
This process adds delay to the speed and power provided by the quantum computer, but the successful end result is more fault tolerant and therefore more powerful quantum computing. But it introduces an additional ironic tradeoff in continuing to build more powerful quantum computers. More powerful quantum computing is generally the result using more logical qubits; but each new logical qubit requires a large number of extra physical qubits to maintain error correction.
The growth in the number of qubits together with their fragility will inevitably require an increase in the delay caused by classical quantum error decoding.
IonQ has announced a new solution to what it describes as this major bottleneck introduced by the classical computer– a new end-to-end real-time quantum error correction decoder running on a single standard classical computing CPU. In its own research published on arXiv, IonQ simulated up to 408 logical qubits across 88 memory blocks and magic factories (functional zones separately handling data storage and complex calculations).
“Under standard operational noise, IonQ’s decoder introduced as little as 0.02% ‘stretch’ time. That means the decoding overhead added virtually no delay to the overall quantum computation,” claims IONQ.
Nicolas Delfosse, quantum research lead at IonQ, added, “Successfully validating real-time decoding across hundreds of logical qubits and over millions of logical operations is an important milestone. Moreover, the fact that our decoder runs on a single CPU provides a practical path to commercial-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing.”
IonQ claims its new error correction decoder confirms the classical hardware overhead does not need to scale exponentially as quantum systems grow wider in logical qubits or deeper in operations, and provides a confirmed roadmap toward more powerful quantum computers.

articles.title: J'ai pris en main le Xiaomi 18 Pro Max : 500 mégapixels combinés, écran de confidentialité et écran arrière dopé — Frandroid
articles.text:
Voilà une famille de terminaux qui feront peut-être date : durant le Snapdragon Summit où Qualcomm a présenté ses nouveaux Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 et sa version extrême, le chinois Xiaomi a présenté ses Xiaomi 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max, officialisés en Chine dans la foulée, ce mercredi 23 septembre. Les deux smartphones reprennent l’écran arrière inauguré l’an dernier par les Xiaomi 17 Pro et 17 Pro Max.
Dans la suite immédiate de l’annonce officielle en Chine, Xiaomi a donc dépêché quelques collaborateurs qui ont volé jusqu’à Hawaï pour nous permettre de prendre rapidement en main ces terminaux.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Meilleurs smartphones 2026 : notre sélection testée, de l’entrée au haut de gamme
            
Les deux appareils se distinguent d’abord par la taille d’écran et le processeur (6,4 pouces et un Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 pour le Pro, une dalle de 6,9 pouces et le Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 pour le Pro Max). Ils diffèrent aussi par leur batterie et par la taille de leur écran arrière (2,7 pouces sur le Pro, 2,9 pouces sur le Pro Max).
Côté autonomie, Xiaomi annonce des batteries silicium-carbone de 7 000 mAh pour le 18 Pro et de 8 500 mAh pour le 18 Pro Max, avec une recharge de 100 watts en filaire et de 50 watts sans fil sur les deux modèles. Ces capacités valent pour les versions chinoises : Xiaomi a l’habitude de les revoir à la baisse en Europe, comme il l’a fait avec le Xiaomi 17.
Une recherche de différenciation
Dès le début de la présentation, le discours de Xiaomi colle parfaitement avec celui de Qualcomm. Chris Patrick, vice-président senior de Qualcomm chargé des smartphones, a en effet justifié le lancement de deux puces haut de gamme parce que « les constructeurs du monde Android veulent se démarquer ».
Une position renforcée par le porte-parole de Xiaomi sur place : « En matière de performances, nous devons reconnaître que les progrès des composants sont souvent simplement itératifs. Il faut plus de différenciation, comme les appareils pliants, gaming, etc. Notre proposition photo et notre écran font partie de cette démarche de proposer quelque chose de différent ».
Et cette différenciation passe aussi par une couche de confidentialité matérielle, présente sur les deux modèles. Elle limite la lecture de biais et peut s’activer automatiquement pour protéger les applications sensibles, sur le modèle de l’écran confidentiel du Galaxy S26 Ultra de Samsung.
iPhone 18 Pro Max à 199€ ! Obtenez 50€ de remise immédiate avec le code NEW50 et jusqu’à 150€ de bonus reprise. Associez-le à un forfait 250Go à 29,99€/mois pendant un an. Livraison offerte.
Finitions impeccables
Avant de plonger dans la partie technique, parlons de prise en main et de caractéristiques esthétiques. Le 18 Pro Max que nous avons eu arbore une livrée bleu nuit constellée de petites taches blanches rappelant une nuit étoilée. Si cela peut choquer sur certains clichés en laissant penser à de petites poussières, dans la vraie vie le rendu est très plaisant et casse un peu la monotonie des tons unis de certains appareils.
En matière de contact, on est bien sur un appareil haut de gamme : les finitions sont impeccables, même si le toucher n’est pas aussi froid que certains appareils concurrents. Les boutons de volume sont fonctionnels, quoiqu’un peu étroits – c’est ici peut-être uniquement une question de goût personnel. Quand on regarde le dos, le cadre supérieur constitué d’un écran englobant les deux modules caméra principaux est objectivement du plus bel effet.
Un écran pour étendre les usages
Si la photo est sans doute un atout majeur de ce smartphone, son écran arrière ne laisse pas indifférent. Un écran qui, bien que petit, est loin d’être au rabais : forgé autour d’une dalle AMOLED de 2,9 pouces affichant 596 x 976 pixels. Il est donc plus grand que celui du 17 Pro de l’an dernier. C’est le Xiaomi 18 Pro qui reprend ce dernier de 2,7 pouces
Celui du Pro Max répond aux normes Dolby Vision, HDR Vivid, HDR10+ et BT.2020 et peut pousser la luminosité à 4000 cd/m² (ou nits) en pointe. Il monte à 120 Hz et propose plus de 100 cartes au lancement (notifications, raccourcis, mini-jeux). Xiaomi y ajoute des mini-applications générées par son assistant IA, comme un minuteur ou une fiche recette.
Ici, l’une des prouesses de Xiaomi, c’est d’avoir percé cet écran pour littéralement y noyer ses modules caméra. Une intégration du plus bel effet, qui offre déjà un premier avantage : la capacité d’utiliser les meilleurs modules caméra pour prendre un selfie.
Si le module avant, composé d’un capteur de 50 MP avec une optique équivalente à un 21 mm ouvrant f/2.2, devrait donner de bons résultats généraux, le fait que la focale soit très grand angle – donc déformante – et que le capteur, au format 1/2,88″, soit un peu petit pourrait toutefois pénaliser les situations de basses lumières. Comme nous le verrons plus bas, le gros capteur du module principal devrait livrer de bien meilleurs clichés.
Deux capteurs grand format
Si nous n’avons pas eu la possibilité d’utiliser les modules caméra, un simple passage par la fiche technique donne directement le ton : Xiaomi a de grandes prétentions en matière d’imagerie.
Commençons par le module mis de côté : l’ultra grand angle. Sous les lentilles, il s’agit de la même catégorie de capteur que le module en façade. À savoir une dalle de 50 Mpix au format 1/2,88 pouces servie par un équivalent 17 mm. Par rapport à ses grands frères, massifs, il est presque invisible.
Il faut dire que ces deux modules sont de petits titans, tous deux de la classe 200 Mpix. Celui qui sert l’équivalent 23 mm f/1.7 est le plus grand, puisqu’au format 1/1.28″, le second abreuvé de photons par un équivalent 75 mm f/2.4 est un peu plus sage (1/1.56″).
Dans les deux cas, cela reste des capteurs plutôt haut de gamme, dont le 75 mm est le plus différenciant. Ce petit téléobjectif capable de « macro » (en vrai, plutôt de la proxiphotographie) sera celui qui produira les beaux portraits et photos de détails. Sans même passer par le traitement cloud dont nous vous avons parlé, il y a fort à parier que c’est le 75 mm qui pourrait faire vaciller les cœurs, avec un capteur vraiment géant pour cette catégorie de téléobjectif.
Un lancement mondial (et plus rapide)
C’est évidemment la question qui brûle les lèvres : ce terminal va-t-il arriver en Europe ? Et si oui, quand ? Pour remettre un peu de contexte, il faut rappeler que l’an dernier, Xiaomi avait fait le choix de ne pas commercialiser ce terminal en Europe, le réservant à son public chinois local – et asiatique dans une certaine mesure.
« Nous tenons à rassurer tous les Européens dans la salle : les 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max seront bien lancés sur votre continent », a expliqué le porte-parole de la marque. Avant d’ajouter : « Pour la première fois, le lancement global sera bien plus rapide que par le passé. Il vient tout juste d’être lancé en Chine et devrait rapidement arriver sur les autres marchés », a-t-il conclu.
La dernière question qui demeure est évidemment celle du prix en France. Un tarif qui sera forcément touché non seulement par la facture de son processeur – le Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, notamment dans sa version extrême, est réputé battre des records de prix – mais aussi par celle de la mémoire.
En Chine, où ils sont en vente depuis ce mercredi 23 septembre, le 18 Pro démarre à 5 999 yuans (environ 780 euros) et le 18 Pro Max à 6 999 yuans (environ 910 euros) en version 12 Go + 256 Go.
Le Pro Max grimpe à 9 999 yuans (environ 1 300 euros) en 16 Go + 1 To, et son édition spéciale transparente atteint 10 999 yuans (environ 1 430 euros). Cependant, ces conversions directes, sans les taxes européennes, ne préjugent pas des prix français, mais on sait d’ores et déjà qu’il seront conséquents.

articles.title: Elastic Beanstalk Adds Cluster Mode, Running Applications on Shared EKS Clusters
articles.text:
AWS recently added Cluster Mode to Elastic Beanstalk, running applications as containers on Amazon EKS clusters the service creates and operates. It sits alongside the EC2-based environment type, now called Beanstalk Standard, and uses the same application, version, and environment concepts. The documentation adds conditions the launch messaging does not mention, covering deployments, cluster access and isolation.
Beanstalk Cluster, as the documentation calls it, is aimed at teams running a portfolio of applications on shared infrastructure. Applications arrive as source code, a Dockerfile, or a container image in Amazon ECR, and source is built into an image with Cloud Native Buildpacks on AWS CodeBuild in the customer's account. Nodes come from EKS Auto Mode, and observability is OpenTelemetry-based.
Customers do not pick the cluster. According to the developer guide, environments in the same account that use the same set of VPC subnets share a cluster, while a different subnet set gets a different one, created on first use in about ten minutes. Customers cannot choose the cluster or its Kubernetes version, and the subnets and cluster IAM roles of an existing environment cannot be changed. Correcting them means recreating the environment.
Direct access to the cluster is not part of the model either. The guide lists cluster infrastructure access as service-managed, through the Elastic Beanstalk API, the AWS CLI, or the console. Paul Pollack, a software engineering manager at AWS, addressed lock-in in his launch post:
With Cluster Mode you can take over management of your application's resources if you ever need to.
The documentation describes what happens when the cluster is changed outside Elastic Beanstalk. The service detects configuration drift, stops maintaining the cluster, places no new environments on it, and fails updates to environments already running there until the change is reverted.
Deployment options are also narrower than the launch blog suggests. It lists immutable and traffic-splitting deployments among Cluster Mode's benefits, but the architecture documentation shows a rolling update, the default, or all at once, and the What's New post lists neither. Immutable deployments remain a Beanstalk Standard feature.
On isolation, network traffic between environments on a shared cluster is blocked by default, with no option to turn the blocking off. The guide still recommends separate subnet sets, and therefore separate clusters, for environments that belong to different end customers, run code the customer does not control, or fall under a compliance regime requiring infrastructure separation:
The controls described in the rest of this topic separate environments on a shared cluster, but they do not make a shared cluster equivalent to separate clusters.
That guidance sits alongside AWS's statement that Elastic Beanstalk is HIPAA eligible and in scope for programs including PCI DSS, SOC, FedRAMP and IRAP.
The economics depend on the same sharing. Elastic Beanstalk has no platform fee and compute bills at EC2 rates, but the pricing page lists two charges Standard does not have: a flat hourly EKS fee per cluster, and an EKS Auto Mode management fee on top of the instances, which EC2 discounts such as Savings Plans or Spot do not reduce. Each load-balanced environment also gets its own Application Load Balancer, and pod-level metrics are metered per resource, which AWS says can make monitoring cost more than on Standard. The savings therefore come from shared nodes, and the guide notes that separate clusters cost more and use capacity less efficiently. AWS's own overview describes Standard as the cost-effective choice for smaller or fewer applications, and as the mode that supports Windows.
The launch also raised the question of where Cluster Mode fits. Replying to the announcement from Dan Ronald, head of product for application integration at AWS, James Eastham of Datadog, an AWS Community Builder, asked how it compares with EKS, EKS Auto Mode, ECS, ECS Express Mode, classic Beanstalk, containers on Lambda and Lambda Managed Instances, adding:
This feels like SNS vs EventBridge all over again
After Ronald replied, Eastham accepted the distinction from EKS and Lambda, but not from ECS:
ECS and Beanstalk Cluster mode seem a little close to each other when they could actually just put a bunch of effort into making one of the services great.
For teams evaluating the mode, the subnet set determines which cluster an environment joins, whether it shares infrastructure with other environments, and how much of the cost saving applies, and it cannot be changed afterward. Applications must also fit a stateless model, with interchangeable replicas and ephemeral local storage, and when subnets are omitted, environments land in the public subnets of the default VPC.
Cluster Mode is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Elastic Beanstalk operates and is not eligible for the AWS Free Tier. It can be deployed through the console, the AWS CLI, the EB CLI, CloudFormation, Terraform, a new GitHub Action, and agent skills.

articles.title: Apple está explorando un rival de Whoop. Lo interesante no es lo que tendrá, sino lo que le quitará al Apple Watch
articles.text:
La empresa de Cupertino está desarrollando prototipos de un dispositivo que apunta a ser, digámoslo sin tapujos, la "Whoop de Apple". Es lo que afirma al menos Mark Gurman en Bloomberg: la empresa ahora liderada por John Ternus lleva meses valorando si entrar en este segmento, aunque todavía no ha decidido si comercializará el producto. De apostar por él, eso sí, tendremos que ser pacientes: no llegará antes de 2028.
Un Apple Watch sin Watch. Los prototipos parecen consistir en una pulsera fina de tela con un módulo equipado con sensores, pero sin pantalla. Sería por tanto una propuesta muy distinta a la del Apple Watch, que combina el seguimiento de nuestra actividad física con la parte de mostrar la hora, notificaciones, llamadas o aplicaciones. En esta nueva solución la tarea fundamental sería recolectar datos de nuestro estado de salud y actividad física, pero sin esa ambición de convertirse en una extensión del iPhone.
Whoop como referente. Las pulseras de este fabricante llevan ya tiempo convertidas en el claras líderes de ese mercado de dispositivos de monitorización de salud. Están diseñadas para llevarlas todo el día y para poder analizar aspectos como el sueño, el esfuerzo físico o la recuperación.
Fuera distracciones, dentro autonomía de la batería. Como no tienen pantalla, el usuario no necesita interactuar constantemente con el dispositivo ni se distrae con él, pero puede consultar esos datos en el móvil con una interfaz y opciones muy valoradas por los usuarios. Whoop presume además de algo que es una ventaja fundamental frente a relojes inteligentes y pulseras de actividad tradicionales: la autonomía supera los 14 días en su generación actual.
La salud no necesita otra pantalla. Si lo que uno quiere es registrar tendencias a medio y largo plazo, importa más llevar el sensor puesto de forma constante que disponer de aplicaciones o notificaciones en la muñeca. Precisamente ahí hay una oportunidad para quienes prefieren llevar puesto un reloj normal, "no inteligente", no quieren dormir con un smartwatch o simplemente buscan una opción más sencilla.
No sería un sustituto del Apple Watch. Apple además sigue trabajando en sus Apple Watch, que acaba de renovar y que se espera tendrán también nuevos sucesores en otoño de 2027. Ahí podría estar la oportunidad de plantear estas pulseras tipo Whoop como una alternativa para quienes no necesitan las funciones extra de los Apple Watch.
La excusa de las suscripciones. Hay otro argumento para crear este tipo de dispositivo: ofrecer algún tipo de suscripción conjunta que permita que los usuarios de los servicios de Apple disfruten de opciones avanzadas para poder sacar aún más partido de estas pulseras. Otros competidores de Whoop (como Google con sus FitBit o Polar con sus Loop) plantean alternativas interesantes, y aquí Apple podría impulsar esas suscripciones que tan buen resultado le están dando a nivel económico.

articles.title: Nosike Nwigene: From tech PR to shaping Africa's AI policy
articles.text:
When Nosike Nwigene was working as a communications professional for tech startups at InsiderPR, a global public relations (PR) firm focused on startups in emerging markets, one of the companies he handled as a junior account manager ran into trouble with regulators.
Max.ng, a mobility startup, had been caught up in a regulatory ban. While others might have responded with a statement or taken to social media to complain, Nwigene wanted to understand what had gone wrong.
“Complaining online is something we always want to do,” he says. “But I was like, this is more than complaining. Something needs to be done.”
That curiosity would take him beyond communications and into policy advocacy. He eventually contributed to the Nigeria Startup Bill, writing advocacy materials, appearing on television to explain the proposed legislation, and supporting efforts to get states to adopt it.
“I am that person who is always curious about a situation and finds the solution to it,” he says. “And this has been part of me throughout my journey.”
That journey, however, did not begin in technology or policy. In fact, neither was part of the plan.
Growing up in Lagos, Nwigene was expected to become a doctor. His father was a doctor, while his mother studied English, and reading and writing were a regular part of family life. His father, in particular, made sure his children spent time with books.
“My dad used to give us tasks before he went out,” Nwigene says. “We would have to summarise maybe five or ten pages of a textbook before my dad would return.”
By the time Nwigene completed secondary school at King’s College, Lagos, in 2005, medicine had already been chosen as his path. He sat the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME), administered by Nigeria’s Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB), hoping to study medicine, but missed the cut-off for his preferred university.
He enrolled at TPP, a preparatory school in Ile-Ife, Osun State, where he prepared for A-levels and rewrote his West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WAEC) before applying to study medicine at Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife. He was unsuccessful.
“So, I left for Abuja,” he says.
After unsuccessful attempts to gain admission to other public universities, including Nnamdi Azikiwe University in Anambra State, his father learnt that the University of Abuja had received approval to begin a medical programme. Nwigene sat JAMB again, gained admission and finally began studying medicine.
“I was in medicine for two years,” he says. “But then, after a few stumbles along the way, I was booted out.”
He eventually switched to Industrial Chemistry and graduated in 2012.
While medicine kept slipping out of reach, another path was beginning to emerge. Nwigene found that writing, marketing and organising events came naturally to him.
“I used to write content for events and organisations,” he says. “I would do anything around marketing and awareness that would bring people to events.”
By the time he graduated, freelancing and communications work had become a regular part of his life.
“I already had an idea of what I was good at and what I would excel at,” he says. “I didn’t know exactly where all of it was taking me, but I knew I could do these things and I knew I was good at them.”
From digital marketing to tech PR
A friend sent him an opening at InsiderPR. After a series of interviews, he joined the firm in April 2019 as a digital engagement specialist.
He developed brand stories, managed social platforms, ghostwrote for executives, and supported clients’ communications and marketing teams. He also worked with startups, venture capital firms, and executives, while sitting in meetings with journalists covering the technology sector.
“Every time the team was carrying out something, I was always carried along,” he says. “They would always put me in meetings with Reuters, Bloomberg, Semafor and so many people covering the tech ecosystem.”
After three years, Nwigene became an Account Manager, leading client relationships and service delivery and advising startups and experts on communications and digital strategy.
More importantly, InsiderPR changed how he viewed his own career.
“When I joined Insider, I realised that there are more professions than doctors and engineers and lawyers,” he says. “Those are not the only professions out there.”
For someone who had spent years being pushed towards medicine, seeing people build careers in communications was significant.
“And I saw that they were making the kind of money that they told me only doctors and engineers and lawyers could make,” he says.
Moving between Lagos and Abuja gave Nwigene a view of the tech ecosystem from both sides. In Abuja, the hub where he worked served as the secretariat for what was then known as the Nigeria Startup Bill, according to Nwigene. At the same time, he was working with a mobility startup facing regulatory uncertainty.
“I could see that this was not an isolated problem,” Nwigene says. “A lot of technology companies were running into questions about how existing regulations applied to new business models, while government was also trying to understand a rapidly changing ecosystem.”
He asked to volunteer with the Startup Bill team and was brought on as a communications officer. He wrote and edited advocacy materials, briefing notes, talking points, articles, and blog posts, and appeared on national television to explain the Bill and its progress.
When the process moved towards state-level adoption, his work expanded to engagements with state governments and Houses of Assembly.
“I was glad we were able to achieve this,” he says. “It is really helping the tech ecosystem in Nigeria.”
Nwigene later received a commendation letter from the Office of the President for his contribution, which he describes as one of the things he is most proud of in his career.
Beyond tech comms
After years of working with startups and technology companies, Nwigene’s work expanded into civic technology and development.
In June 2023, he became a fellow at Code for Africa, a pan-African civic technology and data journalism organisation, working as a digital strategist with partner civil society organisations. One assignment involved supporting work with the African Union on digital engagement, storytelling, and visibility around democratic participation and institutional accountability. He also conducted audience research and capability assessments, Nwigene told TechCabal.
“The biggest thing I took from the fellowship was a deeper understanding of how technology, communications, civic participation and public institutions intersect,” he says.
In September 2024, he began consulting with the Climate Investment Funds at the World Bank, supporting communications around climate investment projects. His work included executive speeches, impact stories, blogs, visual content, social media, newsletters, and communications around programme launches and COP29 in Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan.
The work drew on a skill he had developed throughout his career: making complex information understandable to different audiences.
Building what comes next
Now, Nwigene is building Nonfictly, a small advisory that grew out of the freelance work he started about a decade ago. What began as a name for his independent work has become a five-person team working with startups, senior executives, public sector leaders and organisations.
“Today, I lead a five-person team of writers, thinkers, creatives and problem solvers,” Nwigene says. “We help partners make sense of complicated ideas, tell their stories clearly, get noticed by the right audiences and find practical ways to open doors and get things done.”
He works directly with clients while guiding the team across projects involving communications, stakeholder relationships, government and policy issues, according to him.
That work has taken him deeper into the relationship between technology, government, and regulation, particularly what emerging policies mean for companies building and scaling in Africa. It is also drawing him towards AI policy and governance.
At the 2026 GITEX Nigeria Government Leadership & AI Summit, Nwigene moderated a panel on Africa’s AI compute capacity with Kashifu Inuwa Abdullahi, Director-General of the National Information Technology Development Agency; Dr Lourino Chemane of Mozambique’s National Institute of Information and Communication Technologies; and Dr Mactar Seck of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa.
Over the next year, he wants to deepen his work in AI governance and technology policy, particularly the practical implications of emerging regulation for African companies.
“I’m interested in the space between policy being developed and companies having to operate within it,” he says.
For Nwigene, the journey has also been shaped by the people he has met and learned from along the way.
“I did not go to any conventional school to learn marketing or even do communications. Everything I know, I picked up while on this journey. I learned along the way from everyone I have had the privilege to work with. People have shaped me in more ways than I can count.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Adobe Premiere débarque sur Android avec une appli gratuite
articles.text:
Un an après son arrivée sur l’iPhone, l’application de montage vidéo Adobe Premiere débarque officiellement sur Android. Et, comme sur l’iPhone, Adobe la propose gratuitement aux utilisateurs. L’éditeur, qui entend venir concurrencer des ténors du secteur comme CapCut, promet un outil de montage vidéo professionnel à destination d’un large public de créateurs de contenus.
Une appli de montage vidéo complète et gratuite
Depuis quelques années maintenant, les applications de montage vidéo, qui étaient jusqu’alors l’apanage de puissants ordinateurs, envahissent les appareils mobiles, première source de captation vidéo pour de nombreux utilisateurs. Avec CapCut en ligne de mire, Adobe avait donc dévoilé l’an dernier la première déclinaison de son célèbre outil de montage vidéo pour les iPhone. L’éditeur entend désormais récupérer sa part du gâteau en lançant une version gratuite, mais complète, sur Android.
Car la version d’Adobe Premiere sur mobile n’est pas là pour faire de la figuration. Adobe y a intégré tout le nécessaire pour faire du montage vidéo confortablement sur votre smartphone. L’appli propose une solution multipiste intuitive qui permet de superposer des séquences vidéo, de la musique, des voix off, du texte et évidemment des effets. Elle prend par ailleurs en charge le montage et l’exportation de vidéos jusqu’en 4K.
Adobe y a intégré un outil de découpage permettant d’ajuster vos clips à l’image près, et dispose d’un outil capable de réduire les bruits de fond gênant pour mettre en exergue les voix, notamment sur des interviews.
L’application, qui donne accès à un certain nombre de ressources (modèles de créateurs, transitions, etc.), intègre également des outils d’IA générative de Firefly, comme le remplissage génératif, la création de vidéo à partir d’une photo, ainsi que la génération d’effets sonores.
Gratuite, hors ligne, sans pub et sans filigrane
Pour séduire les utilisateurs, Adobe a mis le paquet. Premiere est utilisable hors ligne, n’affiche aucune publicité et n’intègre aucun filigrane aux vidéos que vous montez. L’application dispose de tout le nécessaire, dans sa version de base, pour vous permettre de monter confortablement vos vidéos.
C’est en réalité sur l’IA générative et le stockage qu’Adobe se rattrape. Car l’éditeur propose des formules de mise à niveau pour obtenir plus de stockage et de crédits supplémentaires indispensables pour utiliser l’IA générative.

articles.title: Grand Prix F1 d'Azerbaïdjan 2026 : programme TV complet et horaires
articles.text:
Grand Prix F1 d'Azerbaïdjan 2026 : programme TV complet et horaires

articles.title: Pangram, una herramienta casi infalible para detectar textos y novelas creadas por IA
articles.text: Un ejemplar del libro "C'etait ca ou mourir", novela del escritor Thelyson Orélien, en una librería en Paris. El libro C’était ça ou mourir ha recibido el premio de novela Fnac, el Medusa y algún otro, lleva más de 35.000 ejemplares vendidos y está entre los candidatos a los grandes galardones del otoño literario. Desde este miércoles, el libro tiene otro mérito: es el primer gran escándalo francés de literatura presuntamente hecha con inteligencia artificial (IA). Su autor, el canadiense de origen haitiano Thélyson Orélien, lo niega. Dice que acabó el primer borrador en 2019 (ChatGPT salió a finales de 2022) y que su tradición literaria “haitiana y caribeña” puede haber causado confusión porque “las imágenes, las repeticiones y el ritmo transmiten una palabra viva”, ha explicado en medios franceses. Su editorial, Grasset, de momento le apoya . La denuncia contra Orélien surgió de una cuenta anónima en X. Seguir leyendo

articles.title: Elon Musk ignoró un consejo de su mamá y hoy es el hombre más rico del mundo
articles.text:
Maye Musk reveló el consejo que su hijo ignoró tras vender PayPal, cuando le preguntó si debía dedicarse a los coches eléctricos, los cohetes o la energía solar. La respuesta de su madre fue simple: elegir solo uno. Algo en lo que Elon Musk no hizo caso.
La anécdota surgió durante una entrevista con Stuart Varney en el programa Varney & Co., de Fox Business, donde Maye Musk repasó los años posteriores a la venta de la plataforma de pagos digitales y la forma en que su hijo terminó construyendo varias compañías al mismo tiempo, en contra de su propia recomendación.
PUBLICIDAD
El consejo que Elon Musk decidió ignorar
Según relató Maye Musk al citado programa, la conversación con su hijo ocurrió después de PayPal, cuando él se planteaba hacia dónde dirigir su próximo proyecto. “Me preguntó si debía hacer coches eléctricos, o cohetes, o energía solar. Y yo le dije: has trabajado muy duro, solo haz uno”, contó.
La recomendación buscaba que Elon Musk concentrara sus esfuerzos en un único sector tras años de trabajo intenso. Sin embargo, el resultado fue el opuesto: en lugar de escoger un camino, avanzó en varios frentes de forma simultánea.
“Así que ya ves, él no me escucha”, agregó Maye Musk con humor durante la entrevista, en referencia a la costumbre de su hijo de tomar decisiones por fuera de sus consejos en materia de negocios.
PUBLICIDAD
La madre del empresario recordó que la decisión de multiplicar proyectos estuvo acompañada de un fuerte escepticismo externo. “Entonces hizo seis compañías, y todas iban a fracasar. ¿Te acuerdas? Todo el mundo decía fracaso, fracaso, fracaso, y ahora estoy muy orgullosa de él”, relató.
Pese a esas dudas, Tesla se consolidó en el sector de los vehículos eléctricos y SpaceX avanzó en la exploración espacial, mientras que la energía sostenible también quedó integrada en sus proyectos a través de iniciativas como SolarCity.
En una entrevista publicada por El País, Maye Musk describió ese patrón como una constante a lo largo de la carrera de su hijo: cada anuncio fue recibido con incredulidad antes de convertirse en un negocio consolidado. “Siempre que tiene una idea, la gente dice: ‘Qué ridículo’. Cuando creó Zip2, la gente decía: ‘Qué ridículo’. Cuando inventó lo que ahora es PayPal, decían: ‘Qué ridículo’”, relató al citado medio.
PUBLICIDAD
La genialidad que Maye Musk identificó de Elon desde la infancia
Maye Musk sostiene que la forma de pensar de su hijo era distinta desde muy temprano. En su conversación con Varney & Co., contó que Elon se sumergía en pensamientos profundos antes de hacer observaciones que la sorprendían, incluso con apenas tres años.
“Podía reconocer cosas, y podía describirlas, y yo pensaba: ‘eso es a los tres años’, ¿sabes? Podía resolver situaciones por sí mismo”, explicó.
A los doce años, Elon Musk desarrolló su primer negocio: un videojuego llamado Blastar, que vendió a la revista PC Magazine por unos 500 dólares. Años después, Maye Musk aportó sus ahorros de 10.000 dólares para financiar Zip2, la primera empresa fundada junto a su hermano Kimbal, germen de la fortuna que consolidaría con la posterior venta de PayPal.
PUBLICIDAD
Más allá de la trayectoria empresarial, Maye Musk insiste en que la imagen pública de su hijo no coincide con el trato que recibe en lo cotidiano. “Es muy dulce, muy bueno. Le encanta estar con sus hijos”, afirmó.
La modelo recordó un episodio en París, durante un evento en el que Elon Musk escuchó pacientemente a un centenar de personas antes de poder cenar. “No dice ‘no’ a nadie”, aseguró.
Consultada sobre qué siente al ser reconocida como la madre del hombre más rico del mundo, Maye Musk remarcó que también es madre de Kimbal y Tosca, y que considera a los tres “extraordinarios”. Sobre Elon en particular, resumió: “Lo que está haciendo es de fuera de este planeta. Literalmente no es de este mundo”.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Lua hoje: confira a fase da Lua desta quinta-feira 24/09/2026
articles.text:
Hoje, 24 de setembro de 2026, a Lua está na fase crescente e 97% visível. Confira o calendário completo de fases da Lua deste mês, de acordo com o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet).
Confira as próximas fases
As fases da Lua no mês de setembro de 2026 começaram no dia 4 com a chegada da Lua Minguante, às 04h52 (horário de Brasília). Dia 11, foi a vez da Lua Nova, que chegou à 0h27. A Lua Crescente surgiu às 17h44 do dia 18. Por fim, vem a Lua Cheia, dia 26, à 13h50.
Leia mais:
- Entenda o que é a Lua, como e quando ela se formou
- Saiba como tirar a melhor foto possível com uma câmera de celular
- 7 dicas para fotografar a lua com seu celular
Calendário das fases da lua em setembro de 2026
- Lua Minguante: dia 4, às 04h52
- Lua Nova: dia 11, às 0h27
- Lua Crescente: dia 18, às 17h44
- Lua Cheia: dia 26, às 13h50
O que é o ciclo lunar?
Uma lunação ou ciclo lunar, como é chamado o intervalo de tempo entre luas novas, é sutilmente variável, com média de duração de 29,5 dias. Durante esse período, ela passa pelas quatro fases principais (nova, crescente, cheia e minguante), e cada uma se prolonga por aproximadamente sete dias.
Também existem as “interfases”: quarto crescente e crescente gibosa (entre as fases nova e cheia) e minguante gibosa e quarto minguante (entre a cheia e a minguante).
Entenda cada fase da Lua
Lua Nova
Na Lua Nova, o satélite se posiciona entre a Terra e o Sol. Isso faz com que o lado iluminado da Lua fique voltado para o Sol, enquanto o lado escuro fica voltado para nós. Por esse motivo, a Lua não é visível no céu noturno. Essa fase marca o início de um novo ciclo lunar e está relacionada ao recomeço e a novas possibilidades.
Lua Crescente
Depois da Lua Nova, surge a fase Crescente. Aos poucos, uma pequena faixa iluminada começa a aparecer no céu, aumentando noite após noite. No início, vemos apenas um fino arco de luz, mas com o passar dos dias a parte iluminada cresce até que metade da Lua esteja visível, momento chamado de Quarto Crescente. Essa fase simboliza crescimento, desenvolvimento e a construção de novos caminhos.
Lua Cheia
Na Lua Cheia, a Terra se encontra entre o Sol e a Lua. Isso permite que o lado lunar voltado para nós receba luz por completo, tornando-se totalmente visível e brilhante no céu. É o período de maior intensidade luminosa, quando a Lua nasce no horizonte exatamente no momento em que o Sol se põe. A Lua Cheia é associada à plenitude, ao auge de processos e à energia em seu ponto máximo.
Lua Minguante
Após a Lua Cheia, a luz da Lua começa a diminuir gradualmente. A cada noite, vemos menos da sua superfície iluminada. Quando apenas metade dela está visível, ocorre o Quarto Minguante, fase oposta ao Quarto Crescente. A Lua continua a perder luminosidade até chegar novamente à Lua Nova, reiniciando o ciclo. A fase Minguante simboliza reflexão, encerramento e preparação para novos começos.
Qual a fase da Lua hoje?
Hoje a Lua está na fase Crescente.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: Eight Sleep's new Pod 6 comes in smaller and solo sizes, starting at $1,999 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the device can be used to adjust the temperature on either side 20% faster than the previous-generation gadget.
Because the new pod has a 50% smaller footprint, it can fit most bed frames. The company claims the device has 9x more sensors, enabling it to understand granular temperature controls for each user even if they are sleeping close together. Plus, it can ignore data from a pet or a kid sleeping on the bed with two users.
The Pod 6 is available starting today in over 37 countries, starting at $1,999 for solo sizes and $2,699 for standard sizes. Solo sizes can fit a twin bed and one side of queen, king, and California King beds. Standard sizes will be available in queen, king, and California King. Plus, it can work with existing add-ons like a blanket, pillow cover, and base.
Beyond new sleep products, the company is pursuing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to transition its Eight Sleep Pod into a regulated medical device for sleep apnea in the U.S.
Earlier this year, the company raised $50 million from Tether at a $1.5 billion valuation. Eight Sleep also took steps to expand its international footprint by launching its product in China, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Singapore in the last year, with China becoming one of the fastest-growing regions.
The company’s CEO Matteo Franceschetti told TechCrunch that international markets contribute over 30% of revenue. He mentioned that the sleep tech company plans to expand into other regions of Asia and Latin America. Franceschetti noted that the company is keeping a keen eye on the component crunch in the electronics sector, but didn’t say whether it will impact pricing.
“We definitely see the market changing a little bit because AI companies are requesting a lot of different components. We are adjusting our supply chain [to counter that]. It’s definitely something that we need to watch out for, particularly as our devices become more and more, I would say, compute-heavy and intelligent to be able to provide AI features to our users,” he said.

articles.title: Small undersea volcanoes may unleash outsized tsunamis
articles.text:
Krakatau, a volcanic island in Indonesia, killed more than 30,000 people when it erupted in 1883. One might assume that volcanic debris posed the major threat, yet many of the victims died from a tsunami caused by the volcanic eruption instead.
Volcanoes at sea can pose hazards quite different from those on land, as their impact can vary depending on how the volcanic activity interacts with seawater. In the deep ocean, high water pressure can suppress explosive volcanic activity, making eruptions less destructive. But closer to the surface, the lower water pressure and the high temperatures of volcanic material can cause violent explosions. Yet scientists still do not fully understand the conditions under which volcanic activity can cause a tsunami.
To better understand these risks, an international team of researchers examined the 2022 Hunga eruption in Tonga, focusing on the rapid caldera collapse that may have amplified its powerful tsunami. Calderas form when the ground above a magma reservoir collapses as the magma drains away. Comparisons of seafloor topography before and after the eruption showed that a roughly 4-kilometer-wide caldera sank by about a kilometer during the eruption.
The researchers argue that the rapid collapse of the entire caldera may have enhanced the massive tsunami. Even a relatively small caldera like Hunga may be capable of producing a dangerous tsunami, depending on the speed and nature of its collapse. This suggests that other underwater volcanoes may also have the potential to generate dangerous tsunamis. Still, the paper warns: “The dynamics of submarine caldera-forming eruptions and, thus, the hazards they pose are not well understood, owing to the relative inaccessibility of the resulting calderas and eruption products.”
A roof too thin to hold
The Hunga volcano’s eruption on January 15, 2022, ranks among the most powerful volcanic events this century. The eruption column soared more than 55 km, pushing vaporized seawater up into the stratosphere, and the pressure wave from the explosion was detected across the globe. The accompanying tsunami is estimated to have reached heights of 40 meters within about 100 km from the source. It is the highest tsunami ever recorded from an underwater volcanic eruption.

articles.title: Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
articles.text:
Meta is quickly iterating on its new Muse AI agent, announcing a bunch of updates today that make the bot more capable and able to chat with you in more ways.
Meta is making Muse more powerful and will let you video chat with it, too
Muse started as a chatbot but will soon be an AI avatar you can talk with over video.
Muse agents are getting their own email addresses that they can use for accomplishing tasks. You’ll also be able to communicate with your Muse agent over the new email addresses, too. In addition, the recently launched Muse Mac app will be getting the ability to use your computer.
Meta is also going to give you another way to chat with its popular AI agent: video calls. Since its recent launch, the primary way to talk with Muse was through a chat interface, but you’ll soon be able to have live video conversations with your Muse avatar. Meta will let you tweak the way your Muse avatar sounds — you can already customize the way it looks — and a new Muse Realtime Avatar model will inform how it moves.
Muse launched earlier this month, and it’s seemingly proving to be a hit, topping the App Store charts and reportedly being downloaded more than ChatGPT on mobile in its first 12 days. Meta appears to be capitalizing on the popularity by quickly introducing the new videocalling features, but that’s not all that’s new for the agent. Meta says it plans to launch Muse on its smart glasses in the coming months, which will let you talk to Muse about what you’re looking at while wearing your glasses.

articles.title: Renault ressuscite la R8 Gordini en électrique, mais ce magnifique concept ne sera pas commercialisé
articles.text:
En 1964, la Renault 8 Gordini se contentait de 95 ch. Son moteur était placé à l’arrière et entraînait les roues arrière. Sa version moderne en a 270 et reste une propulsion, mais son moteur est électrique. Ceux qui rêvaient déjà de la commander vont être déçus. Dans son communiqué diffusé ce jeudi 24 septembre, Renault parle d’un « exemplaire unique » développé comme un pur « exercice de style », qui ne sera pas commercialisé. Dommage…
Ce coupé deux places vient s’ajouter aux autres délicieux show-cars de ces dernières années comme la R17 Electric restomod dessiné avec Ora Ïto et la Renault 5 Diamant de Pierre Gonalons. Tous doivent finir dans le futur musée des Collections Renault à Flins (Yvelines), qui ouvrira au public dans une quinzaine de mois.
Cette fois, le projet a été mené entièrement en interne : un concours au sein du Design Renault a produit plus de 300 esquisses. Deux ont été développées en maquettes à l’échelle 2/5e, puis réunies en une seule proposition. Le choix du modèle n’a rien d’un hasard. La « Gorde » était une sportive dérivée d’un modèle de grande série dix ans avant la vague des GTI, servant de voiture-école à toute une génération de pilotes, dont Jean Ragnotti.
Une R8 Gordini plus large, plus basse et en carbone
Le concept mesure 4,12 m de long, 1,88 m de large et 1,27 m de haut, des proportions proches de celles d’une voiture de rallye actuelle. Ses roues sont plus grandes à l’arrière (20 pouces) qu’à l’avant (19 pouces), en clin d’œil à l’architecture « tout à l’arrière » du modèle original. La berline quatre portes devient un coupé deux portes, avec une carrosserie en carbone et des voies arrière arrière élargies.
Les références au modèle de 1964 sont nombreuses : six phares ronds à l’avant dont les fameux feux additionnels de la version rallye, des rétroviseurs en obus, et la teinte historique bleu de France retravaillé en peinture tricouche. À l’origine, la double bande blanche était un simple autocollant. Ici, elle fait partie intégrante de la peinture et de nombreux éléments sont dans son prolongement comme les grilles du capot, les feux arrière et même la casquette de planche de bord derrière le volant.
Renault souligne que l’habitacle suit l’esprit « café racer », une mode venue de la moto qui consiste à dépouiller une machine ancienne pour ne garder que l’essentiel et la « coursifier ». Renault a remplacé les plastiques par de l’aluminium brossé et de l’Alcantara et, 21e siècle oblige, les cadrans ronds posés sur une lame d’aluminium sont en fait de petits affichages numériques. Les sièges baquets sont recouverts au centre d’un velours côtelé bleu, en référence aux sièges plats de l’époque. Seul le bouton rouge du chronomètre, au milieu du tableau de bord, apporte une autre couleur.
Une fiche technique réduite au minimum
Côté technique, Renault n’est pas très avare en informations : moteur électrique de 270 ch, propulsion et… c’est tout. On ne connaît ni la capacité de batterie, ni l’autonomie, ni le poids (pourtant incontournable sur une sportive), ni le temps pour le 0 à 100 km/h tiens. C’est logique pour un objet de musée, mais quand même un peu frustrant.
On aurait adoré une Gordini électrique de série, mais Renault est déjà bien occupé à développer une autre réinterprétation de sportive, la R5 Turbo 3E, qui doit sortir en 2027.
Pour voir cette R8 Gordini néorétro, il faudra passer sur le stand Renault du Mondial de l’Auto de Paris, du 12 au 18 octobre 2026, puis au musée de Flins quand il ouvrira.
